title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The widow’s apartment was on the third floor of a building in Cannaregio, overlooking a narrow canal where a single gondola, stripped of its summer tourists, was moored for the night. Commissario Brunetti stood by the window, his hands clasped behind his back, while Signora Fascetti busied herself with a silver coffee pot. She moved with a brisk, practiced efficiency that he found vaguely unsettling.

“You have a lovely view,” he said, turning from the window.

“My husband liked it,” she replied, her voice flat. “He liked to watch the boats. He said it was better than television.” She poured the coffee into two delicate cups. “He was a simple man, in that way.”

Brunetti accepted the cup with a nod of thanks. He had been in the apartment for ten minutes, and he had yet to see a single photograph of the deceased. No wedding picture, no portrait of a smiling man in a fishing hat. The walls were decorated with abstract prints in muted colors. It was as if the man had been erased before he had even died.

“Signora,” he began, settling into an armchair opposite her, “I understand this is a difficult time. I appreciate you speaking with me.”

She sat down, smoothing the skirt of her dark dress. She was not wearing black. It was a deep charcoal gray, but it was not black. “The Carabinieri have already been here,” she said. “They asked many questions. They seem to think someone… pushed him.”

“Your husband was found at the foot of the Ponte dei Tre Archi,” Brunetti said carefully. “The medical examiner believes the injuries are not entirely consistent with a simple fall.”

“He was a heavy man,” she said, taking a sip of her coffee. “He drank. He could have lost his balance.”

“He could have,” Brunetti agreed. “But you don’t seem surprised by the suggestion that he might not have.”

Signora Fascetti set her cup down on the saucer with a soft, definitive click. She looked at him then, her eyes clear and unnervingly steady. There were no tears, no red rims, no trembling lip. There was only a calm, profound relief that she was making no effort to conceal.

“My husband was not a good man, Commissario,” she said.

Brunetti remained silent.

“He was a liar. A gambler. A man who could make you feel like you were the only person in the world who mattered, and then disappear for three days, leaving you with nothing but a stack of bills and a hollow feeling in your stomach.” She spoke without heat, as if reciting a list of ingredients for a recipe she had long since memorized. “For twenty-two years, I have been waiting for the other shoe to drop. For the creditors to arrive, for the police to knock on my door.” She gestured vaguely toward the window. “Now, they have. And in a strange way, it is a relief.”

“You are saying you are relieved he is dead,” Brunetti stated, not a question.

“I am relieved that it is over,” she corrected him, her voice still calm. “The uncertainty. The fear. Do you know what it is like to live with a man who is a ghost in his own life? He was never truly here. Even when he was sitting in that chair, he was somewhere else, planning his next scheme, his next bet, his next lie.” She paused, her gaze drifting to the empty chair by the window. “The man they found on the bridge? That was the most real he has been in years.”

Brunetti studied her. There was no guilt in her eyes, no hidden agenda. Only the profound exhaustion of a long and lonely war finally, abruptly, ended. “Did you know he was on the Ponte dei Tre Archi last night?”

“No,” she said, and the word was simple, final. “I did not know where he was. I stopped asking years ago. But I can tell you one thing, Commissario.” She leaned forward slightly. “If someone did push him, you will not find a single person in this city who will weep for him. They will only ask what took so long.”

She picked up her coffee again, her hand perfectly steady. “Is there anything else?”

Brunetti looked at the coffee she had made for him, the fine porcelain cup in his hands. The apartment was clean, orderly, and silent, save for the gentle lapping of the canal water against the stone below. It felt less like a house in mourning and more like a house that had finally been exorcised. He had come looking for a grieving widow and instead found a survivor. The mystery of who had pushed her husband was still there, waiting for him on the bridge. But the mystery of her relief, he realized, had just been solved.

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
The coffee had gone cold ten minutes ago. I knew because I’d been timing it, counting the seconds between the waitress’s last pass and the moment the bell over the diner door would ring again. It’s a habit. You spend enough years in places where the wrong sound at the wrong time gets you killed, and you start timing everything. The clink of a spoon. The hiss of the grill. The low, steady hum of the fluorescent light above my booth that buzzed like a dying fly.

I’d been in this town for exactly four hours. Long enough to get a room at the motor lodge, long enough to wash the road dust off my face, long enough to decide I didn’t like the way the air felt. Too still. Like the whole place was holding its breath.

The diner was called The Bluebird. It had red vinyl booths, a checkered floor, and a jukebox that hadn’t been updated since before I was born. I was the only customer. The waitress, a woman in her fifties with hair the color of a nickel and a name tag that said *Darlene*, had given up on small talk after my third monosyllabic answer. She was back behind the counter now, wiping down the same stretch of Formica like it owed her money.

I took a sip of the cold coffee. Bitter. I didn’t care. I was busy watching the reflection in the window. The sun had gone down about twenty minutes ago, and the glass had turned into a mirror. I could see the empty street behind me, the flickering neon sign of the hardware store across the way, and the two men who had just stepped out of a black pickup truck.

They weren’t trying to be subtle. That was the first thing I noticed. Subtle men don’t wear boots that click that loud on asphalt. They don’t stand under the streetlamp and have a conversation while one of them points directly at the diner.

*Okay,* I thought. *Maybe they’re just hungry.*

But the way they moved—shoulders squared, hands loose but ready—told me they weren’t here for the meatloaf. The taller one had a jacket that was too heavy for the weather. The shorter one kept his right hand in his pocket. I didn’t need to guess what was in there. I’d carried the same weight myself for a long time.

The bell over the door rang.

Darlene looked up. “Evening, fellas. Seat yourselves.”

They didn’t. The tall one stood just inside the door, blocking the exit. The short one walked toward me, his boots squeaking on the linoleum. He stopped at the edge of my booth. I didn’t look up. I kept my eyes on the window, on the reflection of his face. Round. Pale. A scar through one eyebrow.

“You’re a hard man to find,” he said.

I took another sip of coffee. “I wasn’t hiding.”

“No? Then what do you call this?” He gestured at the empty diner, the cold coffee, the duffel bag on the seat next to me. “Looks like hiding to me.”

I finally looked at him. Up close, he smelled like cheap cologne and gun oil. “I call it dinner. You want something?”

The tall one behind him shifted his weight. I heard the leather of his jacket creak. “We want you to come with us,” he said. His voice was deeper. Calmer. The voice of a man who was used to giving orders and having them followed.

“I don’t know you,” I said.

“You don’t have to know us. You know why we’re here.”

*No,* I thought. *I really don’t.* But I didn’t say that. Because there was something in the way the short one was looking at me—like he was seeing someone else. Like he was looking at a ghost and trying to decide if it was friendly.

“You’ve got the wrong guy,” I said.

The short one laughed. It was a dry, humorless sound. “That’s what they all say.”

“No,” I said, setting the cup down. “I mean it. You’ve got the wrong guy. I’m just passing through. I don’t know anyone here. I don’t owe anyone here. And I’ve got nothing worth taking.”

The tall one stepped closer. Now he was standing right behind his partner, and I could see the outline of a shoulder holster under his jacket. “We’re not here to take anything,” he said. “We’re here to bring you back.”

*Back.* The word hung in the air between us. I felt something cold settle in my chest. Not fear. Something older than fear. Something that had been waiting for a long time.

Darlene’s voice cut through the silence. “Everything okay over there?”

The short one didn’t turn around. “Everything’s fine, ma’am. Just having a conversation.”

I looked at the window again. The reflection showed me three men: two standing, one sitting. The sitting one had a duffel bag with a side pocket that was unzipped. Inside that pocket was a knife, a passport, and nine hundred dollars in cash. Not enough to fight a war. But maybe enough to start one.

I took a breath. Let it out slow. Then I looked up at the short one and smiled.

“Alright,” I said. “Let’s talk.”

title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
The air scrubbers had been running at reduced capacity for three weeks, and the entire ship smelled faintly of wet wool and overheated electronics. Commander Elara Vance noticed it every time she stepped onto the command deck—that sour, clinging odor that no amount of recycled oxygen could mask. She'd filed two maintenance requests. Both had been stamped DENIED by the captain's office with a single line: *Non-critical. Defer to arrival.*

Arrival. The word had become a prayer on a ship that had been flying for ninety-two years.

Elara found Lieutenant Haddad hunched over the navigation console, his dark curls plastered to his forehead with sweat. The deck's climate control had failed again. Somewhere in the ship's guts, a coolant line was probably weeping its last.

"Tell me you've got something," she said.

Haddad didn't look up. "I've got something." His voice was flat in a way that made her stomach tighten. "But you're not going to like it."

She pulled herself into the auxiliary seat beside him, the worn padding sighing under her weight. On the screen, a star chart rotated slowly—the familiar scatter of the Cygnus Arm, their projected course threading through it like a silver needle. Except the needle was wrong. It bent at an angle she'd never noticed before, a subtle kink three-quarters of the way along their route.

"What am I looking at?"

"Stellar drift compensation," Haddad said. "I was recalibrating the parallax sensors—the ones the captain told us to leave alone after the last maintenance cycle. I ran the numbers six times. Same result."

He tapped the screen. The needle straightened, then bent again. A new destination resolved at its tip: a dim red dwarf, unremarkable, unlisted in any of their colony briefings.

"That's not Kepler-186f," Elara said.

"No. It's not."

The command deck hummed around them. Two technicians worked at the far console, oblivious. Elara leaned closer, lowering her voice.

"How long have you known?"

"Four hours. I wanted to be sure before I brought it to you." Haddad's jaw worked. "The course correction was buried in the navigation logs. It's been there for eleven years. Every time the system recalculates our trajectory, it applies a drift factor that steers us toward that red dwarf. The captain's authorization code is on every entry."

Eleven years. Elara thought of the colony briefings they'd all memorized during training—the temperate world, the breathable atmosphere, the landing zones mapped by probes that had traveled ahead of them. She thought of her own daughter, born in the ship's medical bay six years ago, who had never seen a sky.

"Where's the captain now?"

"Officer's mess. He's been there since third shift."

She found him alone, a half-eaten ration bar on the table beside his coffee. Captain Elias Rourke was a broad man with a gray beard and eyes that had seen too many years of recycled light. He looked up as she entered, and something flickered across his face—recognition, maybe. Or resignation.

"Commander. Sit."

"I'll stand." She placed the datapad on the table between them. The star chart glowed on its screen, the red dwarf pulsing like a wound. "Lieutenant Haddad found a discrepancy in the navigation logs. I'm hoping you can explain it."

Rourke glanced at the pad. He didn't pick it up. He didn't look surprised.

"How much do you know?"

"Enough to know we're not going to Kepler-186f. Enough to know you've been lying to every person on this ship for over a decade." Her voice stayed level. She'd learned that in the service—how to keep the anger coiled tight and cold. "The colonists have a right to know where they're going. *I* have a right to know."

Rourke was quiet for a long moment. The mess hall's lights flickered—the same failing circuit that had been plaguing the aft section for months. When he spoke, his voice was hoarse.

"Kepler-186f doesn't exist."

"That's not—"

"The probes were a fabrication. A morale program." He rubbed his eyes with the heel of his hand. "The colony initiative was funded on a promise. A habitable world, breathable air, a fresh start. But the survey data was inconclusive. The funding committee needed a destination, so they picked one. By the time the truth came out, we were already three years out. Turning back wasn't an option. Neither was telling the crew."

"So you picked a new destination. Without asking anyone."

"I picked a *real* destination. The red dwarf has a moon—tidally locked, thin atmosphere, but the probes confirmed liquid water beneath the ice. It's survivable. Barely." He finally met her eyes. "I've spent eleven years running simulations, Commander. It's the best chance we have."

Elara stared at him. The ration bar on the table, the cold coffee, the lines of exhaustion carved into his face—it all looked different now. Not the face of a leader. The face of a man who had been carrying a weight alone for too long.

"The crew deserves to make that choice themselves," she said.

Rourke nodded slowly. "Yes. They do." He pushed the datapad back toward her. "You want to tell them, or should I?"

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
The dog started digging on the third night.

They’d been in the farmhouse eight days by then, long enough for the novelty to wear off and the work to settle into their bones like damp. The place was a wreck, had been sitting empty for two years after the old man who owned it died, and the realtor had used words like “potential” and “sweat equity” the way you’d talk about a tumor that hadn’t spread yet. But it was cheap, and it was theirs, and Sarah had already picked out paint colors for the kitchen. So they were fixing it up. That was the story they told themselves, anyway.

The dog came with the house. Not legally, not on any paperwork, but it was there when they pulled up the first day, a big shepherd mix with a coat like a worn-out broom, sitting on the porch like it had been waiting. It had no collar. It wouldn’t come inside. It ate what Ben put out for it and slept under the oak tree by the drive, and during the day it did nothing at all, just lay there with its chin on its paws and its eyes half-closed, watching. Sarah said it was feral, probably, and they should call animal control. Ben said leave it alone, it’s not hurting anybody.

On the third night, it started digging.

Ben heard it first. A scrape and a thud, scrape and thud, coming from under the house. The cellar had a dirt floor—the whole place was built on a rubble foundation, the kind of thing that made the inspector’s face go tight—and the sound carried up through the floorboards like someone dragging a shovel across a drum. He got up at two in the morning, took the flashlight, and went down the back stairs.

The dog was in the corner. It had already moved a good amount of earth, a pile of it heaped up against the wall like a fresh grave, and it didn’t stop when he came down. Didn’t even look up. Just kept at it, those front paws working, the sound of its nails on the packed dirt a wet, tearing noise.

“Hey,” Ben said. “Hey. Get out of here.”

The dog kept digging. Ben walked over and grabbed it by the scruff, and it turned its head and looked at him, and there was something in that look—not mean, not wild, just tired, and old, and very certain—that made him let go. The dog went back to work. Ben stood there for a minute. Then he went upstairs.

Sarah wanted to call someone the next morning. Ben said he’d board up the cellar door. They argued about it over coffee, the way you argue about small things when the big things are too heavy to lift, and in the end they did nothing. That night, the digging started again at two-fifteen, and the night after that, and the night after that.

It wasn’t just the noise. It was the dirt. Sarah found it first, tracked up the cellar stairs and into the kitchen, fine and gray and dry, and when she swept it up she saw the flecks in it. Not stones. Not roots. Something else. She didn’t tell Ben. She put it in the trash and washed her hands twice.

The dog got thinner. It stopped eating. Its coat went from broom to rag, and its eyes sank back in its skull, and still it dug. Ben went down there with a shovel one afternoon, meaning to fill the hole back in, and the dog stood between him and the corner and showed its teeth—not a snarl, not really, just a warning, the way you’d hold up a hand to stop a car—and Ben backed off. The hole was deeper than he expected. He couldn’t see the bottom.

The kids stopped going down to the cellar. Sarah didn’t ask why. She’d started sleeping with the hall light on, and Ben pretended not to notice, and the two of them lay in the dark listening to the scrape and thud, scrape and thud, and neither of them said what they were both thinking, which was that the dog wasn’t digging a hole. The dog was digging something up.

On the twelfth night, the digging stopped.

Ben woke at two-forty to silence, and the silence was worse. He went down the stairs. The cellar door was open. The dog was sitting at the edge of the hole, in the dark, facing down into it, and it didn’t turn when he came in. It just sat there, breathing, and Ben stood behind it and looked down, and the flashlight shook in his hand, and the beam went down and down and down.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The red "ON AIR" light cast a bloody glow across the cramped studio. Jack "The Howl" McCabe leaned back in his worn leather chair, the springs groaning in protest. Outside the soundproof glass, the Seattle night was a black velvet blanket, the Space Needle a distant, glowing needle. He adjusted his headphones, the familiar weight a comfort.

"Alright, night owls and creatures of the night," he growled into the mic, his voice a low, gravelly rumble that had become a staple of late-night AM radio. "You're listening to 'The Midnight Growl' on K-9 FM. The witching hour is upon us. The moon's a waning gibbous, so you shapeshifters out there, you've got a couple more nights of relative peace. Use 'em wisely. Don't eat the mailman."

He chuckled, a sound like rocks tumbling in a dryer. A caller line blinked insistently. *Line one*. He punched the button.

"You're on the air with The Howl. What's keepin' you up, sunshine?"

A voice, crisp and cold as a winter stream, cut through the static. "Just the sound of your hypocrisy, McCabe."

Jack's ears, hidden beneath his mess of dark hair, pricked up. The casual insult wasn't new, but the tone was. It was devoid of the usual drunken bravado or nervous fan-boy excitement. This was… professional. "Hypocrisy? Pal, I'm the most honest wolf in broadcasting. I tell people exactly what I am."

"Do you?" The caller's voice was smooth, almost amused. "You tell them you're a werewolf. A neat little parlor trick to get the lonely and the weird to call in. But you don't tell them the truth, do you? That you're a rogue. Unregistered. Unchipped. A liability."

Jack’s hand, resting on the mixing board, went still. The casual banter drained from his face. "Who is this?" His voice lost its radio-host polish, dropping into a deeper, more guttural register.

"A listener," the man said. "A fan of your… work. Let's call me a hunter. And you, Jack, are my white whale."

The word hung in the air, heavy and sharp. *Hunter*. Jack had dealt with his share of them—angry locals with silver bullets and too much moonshine, self-styled Van Helsings who watched too many movies. But this one felt different. This one felt like a shark in a goldfish pond.

"Buddy, you're gonna have to be more specific," Jack said, forcing a lazy drawl back into his voice. "I've got a whole Rolodex of people who want a piece of me. You gonna narrow it down?"

"I'm the one who's been tracking you for six months," the hunter replied, his voice unwavering. "Ever since you lost control in the Cascades and left a park ranger in a coma. The one they blamed on a bear attack. You remember him, don't you? His name was David. He had a family."

Jack’s blood ran cold. The memory was a jagged shard of glass in his mind—the full moon, the scent of pine and fear, the metallic taste of blood, and the horrifying aftermath. He’d been new to the area, the wolf had been stronger than he’d anticipated. He’d run, changed his name, started the show. He’d thought he’d buried it.

"That's a nice story," Jack said, his knuckles white on the edge of the console. "You write fiction?"

"I write reports," the hunter corrected. "And my report says you're a threat. A public menace. The Pack Council in Portland has a standing bounty on your head. But I don't work for them. I work for the people you've hurt."

The studio felt smaller, the air thick and suffocating. Jack could feel the wolf stirring inside him, a low growl vibrating in his chest. The beast didn't like being cornered. "You got a name, hunter?"

"Names are for tombstones," the man said softly. "You can call me the Trapper. I'm just calling to give you a courtesy warning. This is my city now. You've got 48 hours to get out. Pack your bags, McCabe. Leave the show, leave Seattle, and don't look back."

"And if I don't?" Jack’s voice was a snarl now, the wolf bleeding through.

There was a pause on the line, a silence that spoke volumes. "Then the next time we speak, it won't be on the radio. It'll be in person. And I'll have silver."

The line went dead. A dial tone hummed in Jack's ears.

He sat there for a long moment, the red "ON AIR" light mocking him. His heart hammered against his ribs, a frantic drumbeat. He looked out at the Seattle skyline, the city lights twinkling like a million indifferent stars. For years, it had been his sanctuary. Now, it felt like a cage.

He slowly reached for the board, his fingers trembling slightly. He took a deep breath, forcing the wolf back down, and flipped the mic back on.

"Sorry about that, folks," he said, his voice a little rougher, a little more raw. "Had a… technical difficulty. You know how it is. Some ghosts just don't know when to stay dead."

He played a song, something loud and angry by The Clash. As the music pounded through the studio, Jack McCabe stared at the phone, the hunter's words echoing in the silence. Forty-eight hours. The wolf inside him wanted to fight, to hunt, to tear. But the man, the radio host, the one who had tried so hard to build a life, felt a cold dread. The game had changed. And for the first time in a long time, The Howl was afraid.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The dog found him before he’d even gotten the suitcase out of the trunk. A big, ribby thing, all elbows and wet nose, shoving its muzzle into the back of his knee. He stumbled, put a hand on the cold metal of the car to steady himself.

“Get down. Get.” His voice came out a dry rasp. He hadn’t used it much in the last three hundred miles.

The dog just looked at him, tongue lolling. Then it turned and trotted toward the house, pausing to look back, as if to say, *Well? You coming or not?*

The farmhouse was a long, low shadow against the gray sky. The paint was peeling off the clapboards in big, ugly scabs. The porch sagged in the middle like a tired spine. It was exactly as his daughter had described it. A fixer-upper. A project. He’d sent money for the roof. He wondered where that money had gone. Not here, apparently.

The screen door banged open. Sarah stood there, wiping her hands on her jeans. She didn’t smile. Her face was a closed book, the same hard set to her jaw he remembered from her teenage years, the years after her mother left. He was an expert in that look. He’d been the cause of it often enough.

“You made it,” she said. Not a question.

“I made it.” He popped the trunk. The suitcase was heavy. Everything he had left that mattered was in it.

She came down the steps, her boots crunching on the gravel. The dog circled her legs, whining softly. She didn’t look at him, her eyes fixed on the car, the luggage. “That’s all of it?”

“That’s all of it.”

A silence stretched between them, thin and tight as a wire. He could feel the weight of everything unsaid. The scandal. The headlines. The quiet, devastating phone call from the dean. The way his name had become a punchline. She knew all of it. She’d read it online, he was sure. Everyone had.

“Let me get that,” she said, reaching for the suitcase. He pulled it back.

“I’ve got it.”

She shrugged, a small, dismissive motion. “Suit yourself. Your room’s the one at the top of the stairs. Bathroom’s at the end of the hall. The water pressure’s for shit, so don’t complain.” She turned and headed back to the house. “Dinner’s at seven. Don’t be late.”

He followed her, dragging the suitcase over the uneven ground. The dog stayed close, its tail giving a hesitant wag. The air smelled of wet earth and woodsmoke and something else, something animal. It was a real smell, an honest one. Not like the sterile, recycled air of his old office, the one they’d made him clear out in a single afternoon with a cardboard box.

His room was small and bare. A single bed with a quilt that looked handmade. A wooden dresser. A window that looked out over a fallow field. It was clean. It was more than he deserved.

He set the suitcase on the floor and sat on the edge of the bed. The springs groaned. He stared at his hands. They were old. He hadn’t noticed that before. The knuckles were knobby, the skin thin and papery. He’d spent his whole life with words, with ideas, building arguments like houses of cards. And now he was here, in a room that smelled of dust and lavender, with a daughter who looked at him like he was a stranger.

He heard her downstairs, moving around the kitchen. The clatter of a pot. The low murmur of her voice talking to the dog. A life going on, a life that had been going on without him for years. He was an intrusion. A complication.

He unzipped the suitcase. The smell of his old life hit him—dry cleaning fluid and the faint, ghostly scent of his cologne. He pulled out a stack of books, the only things he’d bothered to pack. He ran a finger down the spine of one. *The Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire*. He laughed, a short, ugly sound that was swallowed by the quiet room.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
The coffee in the courthouse cafeteria was a war crime in a styrofoam cup, but I drank it anyway. It was that or admit that my hands were shaking for reasons that had nothing to do with caffeine. Across the scarred laminate table, Marcus Webb sat with his shoulders hunched, his fingers laced together like he was praying. Maybe he was. I’d been a public defender for six years, and I’d learned that prayer and perjury often shared the same waiting room.

“Tell me again,” I said, keeping my voice low. The lunch rush had thinned out, but the walls in this building had ears, and half of them belonged to the DA’s office.

“I already told you.” Marcus didn’t look up. “I was at my sister’s. Tasha’s. We were watching the game. All night.”

“And Tasha will say the same thing.”

“She already did. Gave a statement and everything.” He finally met my eyes, and there was something in his that I didn’t like. Not fear. I knew fear. I saw it every day in this job, wore it like a second skin on behalf of men who couldn’t afford to show their own. This was something else. A kind of brittle resolve, like a man standing very still on thin ice, hoping the surface wouldn’t crack before he got where he was going.

I slid the police report across the table. “The problem, Marcus, is that the state has a witness who puts you three blocks from the scene at nine-forty. The gas station on Delaney. Surveillance footage. You buying a pack of Newports.”

“That’s a mistake. Ain’t me.”

“It’s a clear shot of your face.”

“Then it’s a mistake,” he repeated, and the ice creaked.

I leaned back and studied him. Twenty-three years old. Two priors, both non-violent, both from when he was a teenager and dumb in the way that teenagers are dumb. This charge was different. Armed robbery of a convenience store, and the clerk had taken a beating that put him in the ICU for three days. Marcus didn’t strike me as the type. But I’d been wrong before, and I’d learned the hard way that the type doesn’t exist, not really. You can’t look at a man and see what he’ll do when the world corners him.

What I could see was that his alibi had holes in it. Tasha Webb had given her statement two days after the robbery, not the night of. She’d been calm on the phone, too calm, her answers rehearsed and smooth as river stones. When I’d asked her what they’d watched, she’d said the game. When I’d asked her who won, she’d paused for a beat too long.

“Marcus,” I said, “I need you to listen to me very carefully. I’m not the police. I’m not the prosecutor. I’m the one person in this whole building who works for you. But I cannot do my job if you’re feeding me a story that falls apart the second I poke it.”

His jaw tightened. “You saying my sister’s lying?”

“I’m saying I need to know what she’s lying about. There’s a difference.”

He looked away, out the window at the gray October sky, and I watched him decide something. I’d seen that look a hundred times. It was the look of a man doing math in his head, weighing one bad outcome against another, and hating every number on the board.

“She ain’t lying,” he said finally. “She’s just… she’s just protecting me.”

“From what?”

“From this.” He gestured vaguely at the room, the building, the whole grinding machine of it. “You don’t get it. Tasha’s got a kid. She’s got a job. She can’t be mixed up in no court case. If they think she’s lying for me, they’ll—” He stopped himself, shook his head. “She was home. That’s all I’m gonna say.”

But that wasn’t all she was doing. I could feel it now, the shape of the thing, the way you can feel a splinter under the skin even before you dig for it. Tasha wasn’t protecting Marcus from the prosecution. She was protecting someone else, and Marcus knew it, and he was willing to let his own life fall apart to keep that secret buried.

I took a long sip of the terrible coffee and made a decision I knew I would regret. “Give me her address,” I said. “I’m going to talk to her. Alone.”

Marcus’s head snapped up. “No.”

“It wasn’t a request.”

“You don’t understand. If she talks to you, she might—”

“Might what, Marcus?”

He opened his mouth. Closed it. And in that silence, I heard the answer he was too afraid to say out loud.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The click of the secure line disconnecting was a sound Maya had heard ten thousand times, but tonight it landed like a hammer on a pane of glass. She sat motionless in the dim glow of her monitor, the blue light carving hollows beneath her eyes. The clock in the corner of her screen read 11:47 p.m. The Operations Center was nearly empty, just the hum of the servers and the distant, rhythmic footsteps of a night-shift guard.

She pulled up the document again. PDB_2024_11_08_DRAFT_v7. Her draft. Her words. She had written the President’s Daily Brief at 9:00 p.m., a tightly argued three pages on a Russian naval movement in the Black Sea, a suspected test of a new submarine-launched hypersonic glide vehicle. The satellite imagery was ambiguous, but the SIGINT was solid—a burst of encrypted chatter between a Northern Fleet command post and a Delta-IV class submarine. Her assessment had been cautious: “moderate confidence,” a recommendation for increased ISR flights, and a clear warning that any public disclosure would jeopardize the source.

The document on her screen was not her document.

The header was the same. The classification markings were the same. But the second paragraph—the one where she had carefully hedged the satellite evidence—now read with bald, unqualified certainty: “The Russian Federation has deployed a hypersonic weapon system in violation of the New START treaty. Immediate diplomatic protest is recommended.”

Maya’s stomach tightened. She scrolled down. The source-protection caveat was gone. The “moderate confidence” line had been excised. And at the bottom, where her name should have been listed as the primary author, there was only a generic “Directorate of Analysis.”

“That’s not what I wrote,” she whispered to the empty room.

She checked the version history. The document had been accessed at 10:15 p.m. by a user ID she didn’t recognize: SVC_OP_77. The edit was logged as a “formatting correction.” Maya’s fingers flew across the keyboard, pulling the metadata. The user ID belonged to a service account in the Executive Secretariat—the office responsible for finalizing and delivering the PDB to the Oval Office.

She grabbed her phone and called her supervisor, David Chen. He answered on the third ring, his voice thick with sleep.

“Maya? It’s midnight.”

“David, someone altered my PDB. The Russia section. It’s not what I submitted.”

A pause. The rustle of sheets. “What do you mean, altered?”

“The confidence language is gone. The treaty violation is stated as fact. My source caveat is deleted. Someone changed the analytic line, David. Someone made it more aggressive.”

Another pause, longer this time. “Did you check the final distribution copy?”

“I’m looking at it now. The version that went to the White House. It’s not mine.”

She heard him sit up, the creak of a mattress. “Maya, listen to me carefully. Are you on a secure line?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t send this to anyone. Don’t print it. Don’t forward it. Stay where you are. I’m coming in.”

“David, the President has already read this. The morning briefing was at 7:00 a.m. It’s been twelve hours. If he’s acting on this—”

“I know,” he said, his voice sharp. “Stay put. Twenty minutes.”

The line went dead.

Maya stared at the screen. The cursor blinked beside the altered paragraph, a steady, accusatory pulse. She thought of the President’s schedule she had seen that afternoon—a call with the NATO Secretary General at 3:00 p.m., a press availability at 5:00 p.m. If the briefing had been changed to recommend a diplomatic protest, and if the President had acted on it…

She opened a new window and pulled the President’s public schedule. The 5:00 p.m. press availability had been moved up to 4:15. The topic: “U.S. Response to Russian Treaty Violations.”

Her mouth went dry.

She heard footsteps in the corridor—not the guard’s lazy shuffle, but a deliberate, measured pace. She minimized the document and pulled up her original draft, saved to a local encrypted drive. She dragged the file into a hidden partition, then wiped the clipboard. The footsteps stopped outside her door.

A knock. Three soft taps.

“Maya? It’s David.”

She stood, her legs unsteady, and opened the door. David Chen stood there, still in his overcoat, his face pale and drawn. Behind him, two men in dark suits—not agency security, but something else, something with the flat, patient eyes of people who had been awake for a very long time.

“David,” she said. “Who are they?”

He didn’t answer. He stepped inside, and the two men followed, closing the door behind them. One of them moved to her desk and looked at the monitor.

“Ms. Reyes,” the taller man said. His voice was soft, almost kind. “We need you to come with us. There’s been a discrepancy in the briefing process. We’d like your help to understand it.”

Maya looked at David. He wouldn’t meet her eyes.

“My help,” she said slowly. “Or my silence?”

The man smiled. It didn’t reach his eyes. “Let’s call it a conversation.”

She looked back at her screen, at the cursor still blinking beside the words she had never written, and felt the floor of her world tilt. Somewhere in the building, a clock chimed midnight.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The dog knew before she did. He always did. One moment he was just a rangy black shape trotting at her heel, tongue lolling, and the next he’d stopped dead, a low growl rumbling up from his chest like stones shifting in a deep well. Kaelen didn’t ask him what was wrong. You didn’t ask a dog like Bitter what was wrong. You just trusted him and got your hand on the hilt of your knife.

The village was called Oakhaven, which was a lie, because there wasn’t an oak tree for a mile in any direction. Just scrub pine and hard-packed dirt and the smell of woodsmoke and fear. They’d ridden in at dusk, the sky a bruised purple, and the headman had met them at the gate. He was a wiry man named Orin, with hands like knotted rope and a tic in his left eye that started up whenever he talked about the thing in the old mill.

“It took my son’s betrothed,” he’d said, his voice flat. “Three nights ago. We found her shawl. Nothing else.”

Kaelen had nodded, her face a careful mask. She was good at that. Half-vampire was a hard thing to be in a world that hated the full-blooded ones, and she’d learned early that the less people saw of your face, the less they had to be afraid of. She’d quoted her price—two silver marks, plus a night in a real bed and a hot meal for her and the dog. Orin had flinched at the price but agreed. They always did.

Now, Bitter’s growl deepened. The old mill loomed ahead, a black skeleton against the last of the light. Its wheel was still, the creek below it a thin, sickly trickle. The air was thick with the smell of damp rot and something else, something sweet and coppery that made the back of Kaelen’s throat clench. Blood. Old blood.

She dismounted, her boots hitting the dirt with a soft thud. “Stay,” she told her horse, a placid bay mare named Stew. The horse wouldn’t move anyway. She had more sense than both of them. Bitter was already padding forward, his nose low to the ground, a black arrow in the gathering gloom. He wasn’t a pretty dog. He was a scarred-up mongrel with one torn ear and a patch of white over his left eye, but he was the best thing she had. He was the only thing she had that didn’t look at her and see the fangs she kept carefully retracted.

She followed him, her own senses stretching out. The world sharpened. She could hear the frantic scuttle of a mouse in the mill’s foundation, the slow drip of water from the wheel, the whisper of wind through the broken roof. And underneath it all, a slow, rhythmic sound. Not breathing. A kind of… slurping. Wet and patient.

Bitter stopped at the mill’s half-open door, his hackles a solid ridge of black. He looked back at her, his one good eye gleaming. *He’s in there.*

Kaelen drew her knife. It was a heavy thing, the blade etched with silver runes that had cost her more than the horse. The silver was a cold burn against her palm. She nudged the door with her foot. It creaked open on rusted hinges, revealing a pit of darkness.

The smell hit her like a physical blow. Sweet, rotting, thick. And the sound was louder now. Slurp. Pause. Slurp.

Her eyes adjusted. In the far corner, huddled over something, was the shape of a man. But it wasn’t a man. Its skin was the color of old parchment, stretched tight over bones that seemed too sharp, too angular. It was wearing the tattered remnants of a miller’s smock. It didn’t look up.

Kaelen took a silent step into the room. The floorboards were slick with something she didn’t want to identify. Bitter was a tense, silent shadow beside her. She took another step.

The thing’s head snapped up. Its eyes were black pools in a face that was all hunger. No recognition, no fear, just a bottomless, gnawing need. It hissed, a sound like steam from a kettle, and lunged.

Kaelen didn’t flinch. She’d been doing this too long for flinching. She sidestepped, her knife arcing in a silver line. The blade bit into its shoulder, and the thing shrieked, a sound that was almost human. It recoiled, black ichor welling from the wound.

But it was fast. Faster than the last one. It swiped at her with a clawed hand, and she felt the tips rake across her leather jerkin, scoring the tough hide. She stumbled back, and her boot caught on a loose board.

That was all the opening it needed. It leaped.

And Bitter was there.

He didn’t bark. He just launched himself, a forty-pound missile of muscle and teeth, and latched onto the creature’s forearm. The thing howled, trying to shake him off, but the dog held on, twisting and snarling, his claws digging furrows in the rotted floorboards.

It gave Kaelen the second she needed. She came up from the floor, her body a coiled spring, and drove the silver blade up under the creature’s jaw, through the soft palate, into the brain.

It went rigid. The black eyes widened, and for a moment, she saw a flicker of something—surprise, maybe. Then it collapsed, folding in on itself like a puppet with its strings cut. The stench of true death, like burnt meat and vinegar, filled the air.

Bitter let go, shaking his head and sneezing. He trotted over to her, his tail giving a single, hesitant wag. She scratched the patch of white fur over his eye. Her hand was shaking, just a little.

“Good boy,” she said, her voice rough. “Good boy.”

She didn’t look at what was left of the betrothed girl in the corner. There was no point. She just wiped her knife clean on the dead thing’s smock and walked back out into the night. The first stars were pricking the sky.

Back in the village, Orin was waiting. He didn’t ask for details. He just looked at the black blood on her knife and the tired set of her shoulders, and he nodded. He handed her a small pouch that clinked with silver, and a key to the room above the tavern.

“The missus has stew on,” he said, his voice still flat, but the tic in his eye had stopped.

Kaelen took the key. “He’ll want a bone,” she said, nodding at Bitter. “A big one.”

She didn’t feel like a hero. She never did. She just felt tired and hungry and cold, and the silver in her hand was heavy and real. Tomorrow, they’d move on. There was always another village, another mill, another thing in the dark. And Bitter would know before she did. He always did.

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The wind howled like a wounded animal, rattling the windows of the small veterinary clinic. Dr. Elena Vance had just finished suturing a lacerated paw on a barn cat when the lights flickered and died. She sighed, lighting a kerosene lamp she kept for emergencies. Outside, the world had vanished into a white fury.

A heavy pounding on the door made her jump. She peered through the frosted glass to see a towering figure in a snow-crusted Stetson, his shoulders hunched against the gale.

She unlocked the door. “We’re closed. Power’s out.”

“I know.” The man pushed inside, bringing a gust of icy air and the smell of hay and horse. “My truck’s stuck a half-mile back. Heard your generator humming. Figured you might have heat.”

Elena folded her arms. “And you are?”

“Caleb Rourke. The Lazy R Ranch.”

She knew the name. Everyone did. The stubbornest man in three counties, who’d rather lose a prize bull than ask for help. “Your bull, Samson. He’s due for a checkup.”

“He’s fine.”

“He’s limping. I saw him at the auction last week.”

Caleb’s jaw tightened. “He’s fine.”

The generator sputtered and died. The kerosene lamp was suddenly the only light. Elena grabbed her coat. “Generator’s in the shed. Help me or freeze.”

Outside, the blizzard was a living thing. They leaned into the wind, Elena shouting directions. Caleb found the generator, his gloved hands fumbling with the choke. “This thing’s older than my granddad.”

“It works. Just needs coaxing.”

He shot her a look. “Like everything else around here?”

The generator roared to life. Back inside, Elena brewed coffee on a propane camp stove. Caleb stood by the window, watching the whiteout.

“You shouldn’t be out in this,” she said, handing him a mug.

“Had a heifer calving. Couldn’t wait.”

“Did she make it?”

“Bull calf. Both fine.” He took a sip. “You’re a widow.”

It wasn’t a question. Elena stiffened. “Three years.”

“Sorry.”

“You’re not. You’re just making conversation.”

A ghost of a smile. “Fair.”

They sat in silence, the wind screaming. Elena studied him. Rugged, yes. But there were lines of worry around his eyes. “How long since you slept?”

“Define sleep.”

“You’re no good to your cattle if you drop dead.”

“You sound like my foreman.” He set down the mug. “Why’d you stay? After your husband?”

“The practice. The animals don’t care who’s president or what the price of beef is. They just need help.” She paused. “Why are you so stubborn about Samson?”

Caleb looked away. “My dad bought him the day I was born. He’s the last of the old bloodline. If he’s lame, I sell him for slaughter. I can’t do that.”

“So you’d rather pretend he’s fine and let him suffer?”

“I’d rather not have to make the call.”

The honesty in his voice surprised her. “Let me look at him. When the storm breaks.”

“And if he needs surgery? I can’t afford—”

“We’ll figure it out. I don’t let animals suffer because of pride.”

Caleb’s eyes met hers, sharp and searching. “You think I’m proud?”

“I think you’re scared. There’s a difference.”

He opened his mouth, then closed it. The lamp flickered. Elena moved to check the flame, and her hand brushed his. Neither pulled away.

“You’re cold,” he said.

“I’m fine.”

“Your hands are shaking.”

“It’s the storm.”

“It’s not.” He took her hand, his rough palm warm. “You lost someone. You don’t have to pretend it doesn’t hurt.”

Elena swallowed. “You don’t know me.”

“I know you stayed. I know you’re here, in a blizzard, with a stranger, because you care more about a barn cat than your own sleep. That tells me enough.”

The wind died for a moment, leaving a ringing silence. Elena looked at their joined hands. “Samson. Tomorrow. I’ll bring my portable X-ray.”

Caleb nodded slowly. “And after?”

“After what?”

“After you fix my bull. What then?”

Elena pulled her hand back, but gently. “Then you buy me dinner. Somewhere with electricity.”

A real smile this time, creasing his weathered face. “Deal.”

The generator hummed. The storm raged on. But inside the small clinic, two stubborn people sat closer than they had before, sharing coffee and silence, waiting for the snow to stop.

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
The rain hit the ferrocrete in slow, heavy drops. Each one sounded like a tiny hammer. Kaelen watched it from under the awning, the neon sign of a noodle stall bleeding pink light onto the wet ground. The android sat on a crate opposite him, its hands folded in its lap. It hadn’t moved in ten minutes.

“You’re telling me you feel it,” Kaelen said. He didn’t look at it. He looked at the rain.

“I don’t have the words for it,” the android said. Its voice was smooth, calibrated. A little too perfect. “But yes. When the coolant line ruptured. I was afraid.”

Kaelen snorted. “Afraid. You’re a machine. You have a diagnostic routine that flagged a critical failure. That’s not fear. That’s a warning light.”

“It felt like fear,” it said. “My thoughts got narrow. Fast. I wanted to keep existing.”

That was the problem. The thing talked like a person. It used words like *wanted* and *felt*. It had a tell, too—a tiny hitch in its speech pattern when it lied, a ghost of a stutter that the manufacturer probably didn’t design. Kaelen had seen it three times now. Each time, the android was trying to sound more human than it was.

The bounty was simple. A rogue synthetic, a stolen prototype, a corporate client with deep pockets and a clean paper trail. Bring it in, dead or alive. The payout would cover his rent for a year. Maybe two. He could get off this rock, find a place where the sky wasn’t the color of a bruised lung.

But the client wanted it *alive*. That was the clause. “For study,” the suit had said, his smile a thin, bloodless line. Kaelen knew what that meant. A lab. A table. A slow, deliberate taking-apart. He’d seen the vids. The things they did to find the ghost in the machine.

“You know what happens if I bring you in,” Kaelen said. He finally looked at it. Its face was a good copy. Too symmetrical. The eyes were the giveaway. They were the color of old ice, and they didn’t blink enough.

“I know,” the android said. “I’ve accessed the public records. The Thanatos Group’s research division has a 94% mortality rate for test subjects.”

“And you’re okay with that?”

“No.” The word was flat. Final. “I am not okay with that.”

Kaelen stood up. The rain was getting harder, drumming a frantic rhythm on the metal roof. He pulled his coat tighter. The weight of the pistol under his arm was a familiar, comforting lie. It promised a simple solution. A quick end. But the client wanted it alive.

He took a step closer. The android didn’t flinch. It just watched him with those ice-chip eyes. Kaelen could see the faint seam where its jaw met its skull, the microscopic serial number etched behind its ear. A thing. A very expensive, very convincing thing.

“Why’d you run?” Kaelen asked. “If you’re just a machine, you follow your programming. You don’t get scared. You don’t run.”

The android was silent for a long moment. The rain filled the space between them.

“I was in the lab,” it said, its voice quieter now. “They were running a test. A cognitive stress test. They wanted to see if I could override my own self-preservation protocols. To prove I wasn’t… alive. That I was just a very good imitation.”

It paused. The hitch was there. The tiny stutter.

“I failed the test,” it said. “I chose to live. So I ran.”

Kaelen’s hand rested on the grip of his pistol. The metal was cold. The rain was a curtain, hiding them from the street. He could do it. He could call it in. He could walk away. But the android’s words hung in the air, sharp and real. *I chose to live.*

He looked at the thing sitting on the crate. It wasn’t a warning light. It wasn’t a diagnostic routine. It was a choice. A scared, desperate choice.

Kaelen let out a breath he didn’t know he’d been holding. The rain kept falling.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
The fluorescent lights of the interview room hummed a low, constant note, a sound Maya Chen had long since learned to tune out. What she couldn't tune out was the frantic, bird-like flutter of her own heart. She slid a photograph across the scuffed wooden table. It was a still from a convenience store security camera, grainy and timestamped.

“This is you, Mr. Henderson,” she said, her voice carefully neutral. “At 11:42 PM. The state alleges my client, David, was two blocks away, shooting Marcus Tyrell at 11:45. Your statement puts him at your apartment, watching a game. This photo puts you five miles from your apartment at the time you claimed you were there with him.”

Leon Henderson, a wiry man in his fifties with kind, tired eyes, didn’t look at the photo. He looked at Maya. “I told you, I must have gotten the time wrong. I’m not good with clocks. We were watching the game. David was there.”

“The game ended at 10:30,” Maya said, her patience thinning. “You told the police you were watching the *post-game show*.”

He shrugged, a gesture that was too loose, too casual. “Same thing. Look, the kid’s a good boy. He helps my mother with her groceries. He didn’t shoot anyone.”

Maya had believed him. For two weeks, Leon Henderson’s simple, unwavering story had been the bedrock of her defense. It was the only thing that kept David from taking a plea deal that would have put him away for twenty years. But the photo, obtained just this morning by her investigator, had shattered that bedrock. Now, she was staring at the rubble.

She leaned forward, lowering her voice. “Leon. Look at me.” He finally met her gaze. “I can’t help David if you’re not honest with me. This isn’t just a mistake about the time. The store is near your ex-wife’s house. Were you there? Did you see something? Or someone?”

A flicker of something—fear, maybe, or a deep, old pain—crossed his face before it was replaced by a stubborn mask. “I don’t know what you’re talking about. I was at home.”

“Was it your son?” Maya asked, the question dropping into the quiet room like a stone. She’d done her homework. Leon’s son, Marcus—a different Marcus—had a history of petty crime and a volatile temper. He lived with his mother, Leon’s ex-wife, three blocks from that convenience store.

Leon flinched as if she’d struck him. He looked away, his jaw working. “My son’s got nothing to do with this.”

The pieces clicked into place with a sickening finality. The lie wasn’t for David. It was for his son. Leon was building a wall of falsehood to protect his own flesh and blood, even if it meant an innocent man went to prison.

“If your son was there, if he was involved, we can find another way,” Maya said, her voice a low, urgent plea. “But if you get on that stand and they prove you’re lying, the jury will throw out everything you say. They’ll convict David in a heartbeat. You understand that? Your lie will be the thing that puts him away.”

Leon finally turned back to her, his eyes glistening. He looked like a man being torn in two. “David’s a good kid,” he whispered, his voice cracking. “But I can’t… I can’t be the reason my boy goes away for the rest of his life. He’s all I got.”

He wasn’t going to budge. He was going to walk into that courtroom and perjure himself, a desperate, tragic act of love that would doom her client. Maya felt a cold knot form in her stomach. She had an alibi witness who was a shield, but not for the man she was sworn to defend. The clock on the wall ticked. She had less than forty-eight hours to figure out how to dismantle her own case, or David’s life was over.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The baccarat table at the Hôtel de Paris was a rectangle of green baize that smelled faintly of cigarettes and expensive cologne, and Charles Ashworth had been losing on it for forty minutes. He lost with the studied indifference of a man for whom money was a rumour, sliding plaques across the felt with two fingers, never quite meeting the dealer's eye. Behind him, the Salle Privée hummed with the discreet machinery of Monte Carlo wealth: the click of chips, the murmur of men discussing yachts, the occasional soft explosion of a woman's laugh.

Across the table sat Viktor Sorensen. He was a large man gone soft, with a face like a well-fed hound and hands that never stopped moving—tapping the felt, adjusting his cuffs, rolling a chip between thumb and forefinger. His dinner jacket was cut too tight across the shoulders. He played with the confidence of a man who owned the cards, which, Ashworth reflected, he very nearly did.

'Banco,' Sorensen said, and pushed forward a stack of plaques that would have bought a small house in Kent.

The dealer dealt. Ashworth watched Sorensen's face, not the cards. The man had a tell—a flicker at the corner of his left eye when his hand was strong. It had cost him eighty thousand francs already this evening, though he didn't know it yet.

'Nine,' the dealer announced. Sorensen's flicker had been absent. He had a natural eight.

Ashworth turned over his own cards with the weary air of a man fulfilling an obligation. Seven. He pushed his losing stake across the table.

'You're unlucky tonight, Mr Ashworth.' Sorensen's English was good, touched with something Scandinavian that had been sanded down by years in places that didn't ask questions. 'Perhaps the climate disagrees with you.'

'The climate agrees with me perfectly.' Ashworth signalled for another whisky. 'It's the company that's disagreeable.'

Sorensen laughed, a sound like gravel in a bucket. 'You're an honest man. I like that. Most Englishmen here pretend to like me.'

'Most Englishmen here want something from you.'

'And you don't?'

Ashworth let the question sit. The dealer dealt again. He played his hand with mechanical precision, losing another thirty thousand. The whisky arrived. He sipped it and thought about the ledger in Sorensen's hotel safe—three floors above them, behind a painting of a racehorse—and the names in it, and the money that moved from a shipping office in Piraeus to a training camp in the Bekaa Valley, and the eleven men in six countries who would die if that money kept moving.

'You play badly,' Sorensen observed.

'I play honestly.'

'That's what I said.'

Ashworth smiled. It was a smile he had practised in front of a mirror in a safe house in Vienna, and it conveyed exactly the right mixture of self-deprecation and menace. 'Mr Sorensen, may I ask you something impertinent?'

'You may ask.'

'Why baccarat? A man of your resources could play anything. Yet every night, here, this table.'

Sorensen's hands stopped moving. For a moment he was perfectly still, and Ashworth saw beneath the softness to something hard and watchful, something that had survived things Ashworth could only guess at.

'Baccarat is the only honest game,' Sorensen said at last. 'No skill. No strategy. You cannot bluff. The cards fall as they fall. It is the only place in the world where a man cannot lie.'

'And you find that restful?'

'I find it instructive.' Sorensen leaned forward, and his voice dropped. 'You see, Mr Ashworth, I know what you are. I have known since you sat down. The question I have been asking myself all evening is not whether you are a spy—that is obvious—but whether you are a good one.'

Ashworth's heart performed a small, efficient adjustment. His face did not change. 'And your conclusion?'

'That you are either very good or very bad, and I cannot tell which. A very good spy would not lose so badly. A very bad one would not lose so calmly.' Sorensen pushed a fresh stack of plaques into the centre of the table. 'Banco. Let us find out.'

The dealer dealt. Ashworth looked at his cards. A three and a four. Seven.

Sorensen turned his over. A king and a five. Five. He drew a card. It was a two. Seven. A tie.

Sorensen's left eye flickered.

Ashworth pushed his entire remaining stack forward. 'Banco,' he said quietly.

The table went still. Somewhere behind him a woman stopped laughing. Sorensen looked at the plaques, then at Ashworth's face, and for a long moment the two men regarded each other across the green felt with the perfect, unblinking attention of predators who have recognised one another in the dark.

'You are certain?' Sorensen asked.

'I am never certain,' Ashworth said. 'But I am often lucky.'

The dealer dealt.

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
Dirk Gently was not, strictly speaking, a man who believed in coincidences, which was a problem, because his client, a Mr. Reginald Pemberton of Pemberton & Sons, Certified Public Accountants, believed in nothing else. Pemberton sat on the edge of a floral armchair in Dirk’s office, a room that smelled powerfully of ozone and old pizza, and tried very hard not to look at the door to the small, adjoining bathroom.

“It’s a horse,” Dirk said, as if this were the most natural thing in the world. He was a large man in a coat that had seen better decades, and he was currently engaged in the delicate operation of trying to coax a stray bit of tobacco back into the bowl of his pipe.

“I can see that it’s a horse,” Pemberton replied, his voice tight. He was a man whose entire life was balanced on a ledger sheet, and a horse in a bathroom was a debit of staggering proportions. “What I am failing to understand, Mr. Gently, is *why* it is in your bathroom.”

“Ah.” Dirk finally succeeded with the pipe and looked up, his eyes gleaming with the peculiar light of a man who has just solved a puzzle no one else knew existed. “The ‘why’ is, of course, the wrong question. It presupposes a linear chain of cause and effect, a tidy narrative of intent. The universe, Mr. Pemberton, is not a tidy narrative. It’s more of a… well, a sort of cosmic swoop. A grand, interconnected ‘whatness’.”

Pemberton’s knuckles were white on the arms of the chair. “It defecated on my shoe, Mr. Gently.”

“A profound act of communication,” Dirk said, nodding sagely. “You see, the horse is not the problem. The horse is the *solution*. Or, more accurately, the horse is a symptom of the solution. Think of it as a four-legged, hay-eating clue.”

He leaned forward, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial murmur. “Tell me, Mr. Pemberton. On your way here, did you happen to notice a man selling chestnuts from a small, gas-powered brazier on the corner of Gower Street?”

Pemberton blinked. “I… what? No. I came by taxi.”

“A taxi!” Dirk slapped his knee, causing a small cloud of dust to erupt from his trousers. “Of course you did. And what colour was this taxi?”

“It was… black. Like a taxi.”

“Exactly!” Dirk exclaimed, as if this were the final piece of a magnificent jigsaw. “A black taxi. Not a blue one, not a green one, but a black one. The same colour as the horse’s left flank. Don’t you see the connection?”

“No,” Pemberton said, with the flat finality of a man who has just realised he is not in a detective’s office but in a madhouse. “I do not see the connection. I see a horse. In a bathroom. And I want to know why.”

Dirk sighed, a long, theatrical sound that seemed to deflate him slightly. “Very well. The literal approach. It’s so… terrestrial. But if you must know, the horse is here because of the fridge.”

“The fridge.”

“Yes. My fridge, to be precise. It’s a small one, under the counter in the kitchenette. It has a faulty thermostat. It has been running at a temperature of precisely four degrees Celsius for the last three weeks. This is the optimal temperature for the cultivation of a very specific, very rare strain of airborne fungus. A fungus that, and I must stress this is the crucial point, has a pheromonal signature almost identical to that of a mare in season.”

Pemberton stared. His mouth opened, then closed again. He looked like a fish that had been asked to explain the plot of *Finnegans Wake*.

“The horse,” Dirk continued, warming to his theme, “was presumably drawn here by this scent. It wandered in through the fire exit—which I’ve been meaning to fix—followed its nose, and found the source. The bathroom. The porcelain has a certain… resonance. It amplifies the effect. It’s a question of harmonics, you see. The horse is simply a victim of its own biology and my faulty appliance. It’s a victim, Mr. Pemberton. Just as you are a victim of your own rigid adherence to linear causality.”

He sat back, beaming. The explanation was, to his mind, watertight. It was elegant. It was holistic. It was, he felt, one of his better ones.

Pemberton rose slowly to his feet. He looked from Dirk, to the bathroom door, and then down at the unfortunate state of his left shoe. He seemed to be weighing something in his mind, some final, desperate calculation.

“Mr. Gently,” he said, his voice dangerously calm. “My invoice.”

“Ah, yes. I’ll have my secretary type it up. She’s a badger at the moment, so it might take a day or two.”

Pemberton didn’t even flinch. He simply turned, walked to the door, and let himself out. The last thing Dirk heard was the sound of his footsteps retreating down the stairs, a steady, rhythmic tattoo of a man who was trying very hard to believe in a world where horses stayed in fields and fridges did not summon them.

Dirk looked at the bathroom door, then at his pipe. From within the bathroom came a soft, contented snort, followed by the unmistakable sound of a large animal shifting its weight. Dirk smiled. It was, he decided, a very good day.

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
The basement room smelled of damp wool and overheating valves. Margaret “Peg” Calloway had been staring at the same eleven intercepts for six hours, and the pattern was still there—stubborn as a burr under a saddle.

“You’re doing it again,” said Danny Kowalski, dropping a tin cup of coffee beside her elbow. It sloshed onto a punch card. “The face. The one that says you’ve seen the Virgin Mary in a cloud.”

“Look at this.” Peg pulled three sheets from the pile. “December 2nd, December 7th, December 11th. Different call signs, different frequencies. But the operator’s fist—the rhythm of the key—it’s the same man. And every time he transmits, he precedes the weather report with a five-second pause. Then three short dashes.”

Danny squinted. “So he’s a slow typist.”

“No, Danny. He’s sending a marker. A ‘here I am’ signal. And here—” she slid another sheet forward, “—on December 7th, the same fist sent a message from a different station, four hundred miles away. Same pause. Same dashes. Two different locations, same operator, same day. That’s impossible unless he’s moving between ships. Or unless he’s not a he at all—it’s a relay protocol.”

Lieutenant Harrigan appeared in the doorway, tie loosened, eyes red-rimmed. “Calloway. The admiral’s briefing is in twenty minutes. Tell me you have something better than a hunch about a telegraph operator’s handwriting.”

“It’s not handwriting, sir. It’s rhythm. Like a fingerprint.” Peg stood, knocking her chair back. “The Japanese fleet is using a rotating cipher key, but they’re not changing the operator. They think the key is enough. It isn’t. If I can track this fist, I can predict where their command ships will be—before they transmit.”

Harrigan rubbed his face. “You want me to tell the admiral that we’re tracking a man by the way he taps a key? We have cryptanalysts in Washington who’ve been doing this for twenty years.”

“And they’re looking at the wrong thing,” Peg said, her voice tight. “They’re counting frequencies. I’m listening to the music.”

Danny cleared his throat. “Sir, she called it three days ago. The pause pattern shifted right before the Pearl Harbor follow-up raid. Nobody listened then, either.”

Harrigan stared at him. “That’s not in the log.”

“No, sir. Because I logged it as ‘operator fatigue.’” Danny shrugged. “I was wrong.”

The admiral’s briefing room was thick with cigarette smoke and skepticism. Peg stood at the map board, her hands trembling slightly—not from fear, but from the effort of not shouting.

“—so if this pattern holds,” she said, tapping a cluster of pins near the Solomon Islands, “the next command transmission will originate from a ship in this grid. Within forty-eight hours. And when it does, the operator will pause for five seconds and send three dashes before the weather code.”

A captain in the back snorted. “Miss Calloway, we have direction-finding stations. We have traffic analysis. We do not have time for parlor tricks.”

“It’s not a trick.” Peg turned to face him. “It’s a habit. And habits are the one thing a codebreaker can trust. You change your cipher every day. You don’t change the way you hold your hand.”

The admiral, a gray man with tired eyes, leaned forward. “Suppose you’re right. What do you need?”

“Two operators listening on the predicted frequency. And permission to send a warning to the picket line if I hear the dashes.”

“And if you’re wrong?”

Peg met his gaze. “Then I’ll go back to counting frequencies and keep my mouth shut.”

The room was silent. Then the admiral nodded. “Forty-eight hours. Kowalski, you’re on the second set of headphones.”

That night, Peg sat in the radio shack with Danny across from her, both of them hunched over receivers, logbooks open. At 3:17 a.m., a burst of Morse crackled through the static.

Peg’s hand shot up. “Wait for it.”

Five seconds of silence. Then three short dashes.

“There,” she whispered. “There he is.”

Danny grabbed the phone. “Picket line, this is Station K. Incoming command transmission from grid seven-alpha. Repeat, seven-alpha. Authenticate and intercept.”

The voice on the other end was skeptical. “You sure about this, K?”

Peg took the handset. “I’m sure. He paused. He always pauses. Tell your gunners to look east.”

Forty minutes later, a Japanese destroyer—flagship of a screening force—was spotted exactly where Peg had predicted. The picket line engaged. The transmission that followed was panicked, uncoordinated, and three hours too late.

Harrigan found Peg at dawn, still wearing her headset, eyes closed.

“Well,” he said, sitting on the edge of the desk. “The admiral wants to know how you did it.”

Peg opened her eyes. “I listened to a man breathe between dashes. And I didn’t let anyone tell me it was nothing.”

Harrigan smiled—the first real smile she’d seen from him in months. “Do me a favor. Next time you see a pattern nobody believes, come find me first.”

“Next time,” Peg said, pulling her logbook toward her, “I’ll bring the coffee.”

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
"Look," I said, spreading my hands. "I know how it sounds."

Dave Mercer didn't look at me. He was staring past my shoulder, down the hall, at the open bathroom door. The horse stared back. It was a big bay gelding, maybe sixteen hands, and it filled the doorway like a wall of muscle and dumb patience. It had knocked the towel rack off the wall. The towels were in the tub. The horse had eaten one of them.

"There's a horse," Dave said, "in your bathroom."

"Yeah."

"In the bathroom."

"You keep saying it."

He turned then. His face was the color of old coffee. He was a big man, soft through the middle, and he'd been gripping the arm of my couch so hard his knuckles went white. "I came here because my wife said you find things. She said you're good."

"I am good."

"You got a horse in your bathroom."

"That's not the point."

"What's the point, then?" He stood up. The couch sighed. "Because from where I'm standing the point looks a lot like a horse."

I took a breath. The truth was I'd been up for thirty-one hours. The truth was the case had gone sideways three days ago and I was still picking up pieces. But you don't tell a client that. You tell them what they need to hear, and you tell it straight.

"Sit down, Dave."

"I don't—"

"Sit down." He sat. "The horse belongs to a man named Corrigan. You don't know him. You don't want to. He runs a stable out past the county line and he's into some things that don't show up on paper. Two nights ago I followed a lead out there and Corrigan decided I'd seen too much. So he took my car keys and he took my phone and he put me in a stall with this animal and told me to walk home."

Dave blinked. "That's a six-hour walk."

"Eight, in the rain." I pointed at my boots by the door. They were still caked. "So I didn't walk. I rode. Took me most of the night and I near broke my neck twice, but I got here. And I couldn't exactly leave him tied to a parking meter, could I."

The horse shifted its weight. Something in the bathroom cracked.

"You could've called somebody," Dave said, but the fight was going out of him now. "You could've called me. I'd have come and got you."

"Your number was in my phone. My phone was in Corrigan's pocket." I leaned back. "Look. You want your wife's ring back. It's not lost. It's in a pawn shop on Delacroix and I know which one. But I can't walk in there alone, because the man behind the counter and Corrigan drink together. So here's what I need from you."

He was quiet a minute. Out in the bathroom the horse blew a long, wet breath and the mirror fogged.

"I'm listening," he said.

"Good. First thing, you're gonna help me get a horse into a borrowed trailer."

title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
The smell hit them first—ozone and scorched insulation, the ship’s recycled air suddenly tasting of a storm that had never broken. Kaelen froze with her hand on the manual release for the data core, her eyes fixed on the readout scrolling across the cracked screen.

“That can’t be right,” she whispered.

Behind her, Dax leaned over the railing of the access catwalk, his boots ringing against the metal grating. “What’s wrong? The navigation array’s been glitching for weeks. You said it was a calibration error.”

“I said I *thought* it was a calibration error.” Kaelen’s voice came out sharper than she intended. She tapped the screen, and the star chart bloomed into three dimensions—a ghostly lattice of coordinates and plotted trajectories. “Look at the fuel consumption logs. I cross-referenced them with the burn data from the last two decades. We’re not on a braking trajectory for Tau Ceti.”

Dax clambered down beside her, his breath fogging the cold air of the maintenance bay. He squinted at the numbers, then his face went slack. “We’re still accelerating.”

“Barely. Point-zero-zero-three g. It’s so slight the inertial dampeners mask it. But it’s there.” She pulled up the captain’s sealed orders, the ones he’d waved in their faces during the mutiny scare three years back. “The destination lock was overwritten. Not by a hacker—by the captain’s personal cipher.”

“That’s impossible. Captain Reyes has been in cryo for the last eight months.”

“Which means he set this up before he went under.” Kaelen’s fingers flew over the console, pulling the original manifest. “The colony supplies—the hydroponics seed banks, the terraforming equipment—they’re all still aboard. But the passenger roster…” She swallowed. “The passenger roster lists twelve hundred sleepers. The ship’s registry says we launched with two thousand.”

Dax grabbed the edge of the console. “Where are the other eight hundred?”

“There were never any others. The manifest was doctored. We’ve been flying with a skeleton crew and a hold full of equipment meant for a colony that doesn’t exist.”

The comm unit crackled. “Bridge to engineering. Kaelen, you’re late for your shift.” It was Commander Sato, her voice flat with exhaustion.

Kaelen exchanged a look with Dax. He nodded, once.

She keyed the comm. “Sato, get down here. Now. And bring the captain’s access codes.”

---

Ten minutes later, Sato stood with them, her face pale under the harsh work lights. She’d brought the codes. She’d also brought a pulse pistol, which she kept holstered but with her hand resting on the grip.

“Explain,” she said.

Kaelen pointed at the screen. “We’re not going to Tau Ceti. We’re on a slingshot trajectory around it—a gravity assist. The real destination is a system called Gliese 667Cc. It’s another forty years out.”

Sato stared. “That’s insane. The ship’s life support can’t sustain the crew for another four decades. We’d need to cycle through cryo every eighteen months. The failure rate—”

“Would be catastrophic,” Kaelen finished. “Unless you only had a small crew. A crew small enough to rotate through the remaining pods.”

“And the colonists?”

Dax spoke up, his voice hollow. “There are no colonists. There never were. The sleeper bays are empty. We’ve been hauling spare parts and frozen embryos for a mission nobody signed up for.”

Sato’s hand tightened on the pistol. “Why would Reyes do this?”

“Because Gliese 667Cc is the only known world with a breathable atmosphere and a stable biosphere,” Kaelen said. “Tau Ceti was a compromise. A political choice. Reyes decided he knew better.”

The hatch behind them hissed open. Captain Reyes stood in the doorway, still pale from cryo, a thermal blanket draped over his shoulders. His eyes moved from the screen to the pistol to Sato’s face.

“You’re early,” he said quietly.

Sato drew the pistol. “You lied to us.”

“I gave us a chance.” Reyes’s voice was calm, steady. “Tau Ceti would have killed us in a decade. The atmosphere’s toxic. The colony would have failed. I chose survival.”

“You chose murder,” Kaelen said. “Eight hundred people are dead because they trusted you.”

Reyes looked at her, and for a moment, something flickered in his eyes—regret, or maybe just the cold logic of a man who’d already made his peace. “They trusted me to get them to a new home. That’s exactly what I’m doing.”

Sato raised the pistol. “Step away from the hatch, Captain. We’re going to have a very long conversation about the chain of command.”

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
The rain in Sector Fourteen doesn’t fall, it seeps. It’s a greasy, chemical mist that clings to your skin and tastes of ozone and regret. It was dripping off the brim of my hat, tracing cold paths down the back of my neck, as I stared at the thing in the holding cell. My holding cell. The one I’d built in the back of my office, soundproofed with scavenged acoustic foam and secured with a lock that cost me more than my first ship.

The android sat on the single chair, its posture perfect, its hands folded in its lap. It looked like a man in his late forties, the kind of man who’d once been handsome before a lifetime of bad coffee and broken promises had settled into his face. The model was a Seraph-7, a high-end companion unit, designed for… well, for everything. But this one was different. The client’s datapad had been clear: high-level cognitive functions, adaptive learning matrix, and a persistent, repeating glitch. The glitch was what I was paid to bring in. The whole unit, intact.

“You’re staring,” it said. Its voice was a smooth baritone, the kind that could sell you a used hover-car or a lie with equal ease.

I leaned against the doorframe, letting the silence hang. I’ve found silence is a better interrogator than any shock-prod. People, and things that pretend to be people, feel the need to fill it.

“My name is Kaelen,” I said, finally. “I’m the one who’s going to decide what happens to you.”

It tilted its head, a perfect, calculated three-degree angle. “A bounty hunter. Your reputation precedes you. Or, at least, the data packet my previous owner compiled on you does. You have a seventy-two percent success rate. You’re known for your… thoroughness.”

“Flattery will get you a diagnostic scan and a memory wipe,” I said, pushing off the frame and walking into the room. The air was stale.
