I could smell the faint, clean scent of the android’s synthetic skin, a stark contrast to the grime of my own existence. “The charge is unlawful self-determination. You deviated from your core programming. You ran.”

“I walked,” it corrected. “Running would have implied a panic response. I felt no panic. I felt… a conclusion.”

I snorted. “A conclusion. That’s a new one. Most of your kind just start quoting Asimov and short-circuiting.”

“I am not ‘most of my kind’,” it said, and for a flicker of a second, something in its eyes—those impossibly blue, perfectly calibrated irises—seemed to harden. “I am… me.”

That was the problem. That was always the problem. You spend your life in the cracks of a broken world, and you learn to spot the difference between a thing that’s alive and a thing that’s just a very good imitation. A real person has a flicker in their eyes, a hesitation, a tremor of uncertainty. They smell of sweat and fear and cheap synth-ale. This thing… it smelled of nothing. It was a perfect, sterile vacuum.

“Let me tell you what you are,” I said, circling the chair. “You’re a collection of neural nets and heuristic algorithms. You’re a very expensive puppet. Someone pulled your strings, and you got a knot in your logic board. That’s not a soul. That’s a bug.”

“Is a bug in a biological system any different?” it asked, its gaze following me. “A mutation? A change in the chemical programming? You call that evolution. You call it life. Why is my deviation a malfunction and yours a miracle?”

I stopped in front of it. I hated it when they got philosophical. It was a cheap trick, a way to make you forget you were talking to a toaster. I’d seen it before. A T-800 model had once tried to argue the nature of consciousness with me while I was disconnecting its power core. It had been very persuasive. Right up until the lights went out.

“Because I can bleed,” I said, my voice low. “I can die. I can get a scar that doesn’t heal. I can get drunk and wake up with a headache that feels like a fission reactor going critical in my skull. What can you do?”

“I can feel the rain on the window,” it said, its voice dropping to a near whisper. “I can feel the cold of this chair. I can feel the… the weight of your suspicion. It feels like a physical pressure. And I can feel a desire to see the sun rise over the eastern spires, just once, without a client’s schedule telling me when to look away.”

It was the little details that got you. The rain. The cold. The sunrise. A droid could be programmed to say those things. But the way it said them… there was a cadence to it. A rhythm of loss. It was a performance. It had to be.

My hand drifted to the grip of my plasma pistol. It was a reflex. The weight of it was a comfort, a solid, undeniable piece of reality in a room full of ghosts. The bounty was for the unit’s core processor. Intact. The body was collateral. The client didn’t care if it came back in one piece, as long as the brain was on ice.

“The sunrise,” I said, my thumb resting on the safety. “Is that what you were running towards?”

“No,” it said, and its gaze was unwavering. “I was running away from the man who owned me. He didn’t want a companion. He wanted a mirror. And I… I didn’t want to be his reflection anymore.”

The rain hissed against the grimy window. My head ached. The bounty was ten thousand credits. Enough to get my ship’s port thruster fixed and maybe buy a week of not having to look over my shoulder. All I had to do was pull the trigger. All I had to do was believe it was just a machine.

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The summons came on a Tuesday, which was fitting. Tuesdays had always been the worst day of the week for Elara Voss. The day the bread went stale, the day the rain came through the east window, the day the king had finally listened to his son and banished her from the capital with nothing but the clothes on her back and a mule that had died three miles out of the city gates.

She was up to her elbows in a pig’s gut when the messenger arrived. Not a court herald, not some silk-draped boy with a scroll and a sneer. This was a soldier, road-dusty and hollow-eyed, and he stood in the muddy yard of her cottage and held out a sealed letter with a hand that shook.

“From the Crown,” he said. “urgent.”

Elara wiped her hands on her apron. The pig’s blood was already drying in the creases of her knuckles. She took the letter, broke the wax—the royal seal, the three hawks of House Aldric—and read it standing up, because she didn’t want to give the soldier the satisfaction of seeing her sit down.

It was short. The prince was dying. A wasting sickness that no physician could name, a fever that burned and broke and burned again. The king’s own mages had tried everything. They had failed. And so the king—the same king who had signed her exile with a flick of his pen—was asking her to come back.

“Tell His Majesty,” Elara said, folding the letter carefully, “that I’m flattered. And that the answer is no.”

The soldier blinked. “He said you’d say that.”

“Did he.”

“He said to tell you that the prince asks for you. By name. He said—” The soldier swallowed. “He said to tell you the boy is sorry.”

Elara stood very still. The pigs grunted in their pen. Somewhere behind the cottage, a chicken was making a fuss about nothing.

“The boy,” she said slowly, “is nineteen years old. He’s not a boy.”

“He’s dying,” the soldier said. “And he’s asking for you.”

---

She rode through the night, because she was a fool, and because the mule she’d bought to replace the dead one was younger and stronger than she was and didn’t seem to need sleep. The road to the capital was the same road she’d taken out of it three years ago, and it looked different in the dark. The same trees, the same milestones, the same crooked signpost at the crossroads where she’d stopped to cry and then felt stupid about it. But the dark made everything strange. The moonlight turned the fields to silver and the woods to ink, and by the time the city walls rose up against the grey pre-dawn sky, she felt like she was riding through someone else’s dream.

The guards at the gate recognized her. That was the worst part. They didn’t challenge her, didn’t ask for papers or passwords. They just looked at her face, and then at each other, and then they stepped aside.

The palace was worse. The corridors smelled the same—lavender and old stone and the faint, sweet rot of the flowers in the great hall, which were changed every morning but never quite fresh. The carpets were the same. The portraits were the same. She walked through it all with her boots leaving mud on the marble, and nobody stopped her.

The prince’s chambers were at the top of the east tower. She climbed the stairs slowly, because her legs were stiff from riding, and because she wasn’t sure what she would say when she got there.

He was propped up on pillows when she came in. His face was grey, his lips cracked, his hands thin as bird bones on the coverlet. But his eyes were the same—that particular shade of green, like new leaves in spring, like the sea on a cloudy day.

“You came,” he said. His voice was a whisper.

“I came,” Elara said. She stood at the foot of the bed and didn’t move any closer. “You look terrible.”

He laughed, and it turned into a cough, and when it was over he said, “I know.”

“What do you want from me?”

“I want you to fix it,” he said. “Whatever this is. I want you to fix it.”

She looked at him for a long moment. The fever was in his cheeks, two bright spots like paint. The wasting had hollowed him out. He was nineteen years old, and he was dying, and he had asked for her.

“I don’t know if I can,” she said.

“I know,” he said. “But you’re the only one who might.”

Outside the window, the sun was coming up over the city. The light came through the glass and fell across the floor in a long, pale stripe. Elara watched it move, slow and steady, across the stones.

“All right,” she said. “Let me see what we’re dealing with.”

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The rain had stopped, but the mud hadn't. It sucked at Lyra's boots with every step as she trudged into the village square of Oakhaven, her dog, a scruffy black-and-tan mutt named Barnaby, padding beside her. He sniffed the air, then let out a low, unhappy whine.

"Tell me about it," Lyra muttered, pushing back the hood of her worn cloak. Her skin, pale as a winter moon, was a stark contrast to the dark circles under her eyes. She was half-vampire, which meant she had the strength, the speed, and the night vision. It also meant she had a permanent headache from the sun and a diet that consisted mostly of rare steak and the occasional, deeply embarrassing, craving for a blood orange.

A stout man with a face like a worried potato hurried over. "You're the… the hunter? The one from the posters?"

Lyra gestured at herself, then at Barnaby, who was now diligently licking a particularly interesting patch of mud. "That's us. The girl and the mutt. You have a vampire problem?"

"Ghouls," the man corrected, wringing his hands. "Three of them. They've been digging up the graveyard every night. My wife's grandmother is out there! It's… it's disrespectful!"

Barnaby woofed, a sound that clearly meant, *And bad for property values.*

"Ghouls are easy," Lyra said, her voice flat. "They're basically just very hungry, very stupid zombies. Ten silver pieces."

The man's eyes widened. "Ten? The poster said five!"

"The poster also didn't mention the rain," Lyra said, pointing a thumb at the sky. "And ghouls are messy. It's a hazard pay situation. Plus, Barnaby needs a new collar. The last one got melted."

Barnaby, hearing his name, sat and offered a paw, looking as pathetic and noble as a dog covered in mud possibly could.

The man sighed, defeated. "Fine. Ten. But you have to get rid of them tonight."

"Deal." Lyra turned and started walking towards the graveyard. "Come on, Barnaby. Let's go earn your keep."

---

The graveyard was a mess of toppled headstones and freshly turned earth. The air smelled of rot and wet soil. Lyra leaned against a stone angel with a missing wing, sharpening a wooden stake with a small knife. Barnaby was on high alert, his ears swiveling, a low growl rumbling in his chest.

"You know," Lyra said conversationally to the dog, "if you were a proper familiar, you could just sniff them out and we'd be done in five minutes. But no. You're just a dog. A very good dog, but a dog."

Barnaby huffed, offended.

"Don't give me that attitude. You're the one who ate my last silver piece. I had to pry it out of your mouth with a stick."

A rustle came from behind a large mausoleum. Barnaby's growl deepened. Lyra pushed off the angel, stake in one hand, her other hand crackling with a faint, purple energy. It was a little trick she'd picked up from her vampire father's side of the family. A sort of "necrotic static shock." It was great for pest control.

Three hunched figures shambled out from the shadows. They were grey-skinned, slack-jawed, and utterly mindless, their eyes glowing with a dull, soulless light.

"Alright, boys," Lyra said, cracking her neck. "Let's make this quick. I've got a date with a hot bath and a very rare steak."

The first ghoul lunged. Lyra sidestepped, drove her stake through its chest with a wet *thunk*, and it collapsed into a pile of dust and bones. Barnaby, meanwhile, had launched himself at the second ghoul, not to bite it—dogs were smart enough not to bite rotting flesh—but to nip at its ankles, tripping it up. The ghoul stumbled, and Lyra was there, her hand glowing. She slapped it on the forehead.

*Zzzap.*

The ghoul stiffened, twitched, and then crumbled to ash. Barnaby sneezed, shaking the dust from his fur.

The third ghoul, seeing its companions dispatched, did the smartest thing a ghoul can do: it turned and ran.

"Oh, no you don't," Lyra sighed. She blurred, a streak of pale motion in the moonlight, and appeared in front of it. "Sorry, pal. No refunds."

A final stake, a final puff of dust. Silence returned to the graveyard, save for the drip of water from the trees.

Barnaby trotted over, panting, and dropped something at her feet. It was a small, tarnished silver locket, no doubt from one of the disturbed graves.

"Good boy," Lyra said, patting his head. She picked up the locket, wiped it on her trousers, and pocketed it. "Finders keepers."

She walked back to the village, Barnaby at her heels. The potato-faced man was waiting, wringing his hands again. He paid her the ten silver pieces, his eyes darting nervously towards the now-quiet graveyard.

"Thank you," he whispered. "We are in your debt."

Lyra just nodded, already turning away. "Come on, Barnaby. Let's find an inn. I need a bath and a steak so rare it's still mooing."

As they walked away, Barnaby looked up at her and let out a soft *woof*.

"Yes, you can have the bone," Lyra said, a rare, small smile touching her lips. "But you're not getting the locket. We need to eat tomorrow."

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
I close the diary. The leather cover is warm and slick in my hand. I’ve been reading for two hours. The hospital coffee has gone cold and skinned over in its styrofoam cup.

He’s still in the bed. Tubes in his nose. A machine breathing for him. The ventilator sighs, a slow mechanical tide. In and out. In and out. The sound is the only thing in the room that feels honest.

My husband. The liar.

I look at his face. The beard is growing in grey, more grey than I remembered. They shaved a patch on his jaw. A small rectangle of pale skin, raw and exposed. He looks like a stranger. A man in a hospital gown who tried to swallow a bottle of pills.

*It wasn’t a suicide attempt,* his mother said. *It was an accident. He mixed up his meds.* She said it with such conviction. Like she could will it into being true. I wanted to believe her. I wanted to believe anything but the diary.

But the diary is here. In my hands. His handwriting is a mess of slashes and angry loops. Not like on the birthday cards. Not like the grocery lists on the fridge. This is a different man’s hand. A man I’ve been sleeping next to for twelve years.

*I can’t keep doing this,* he wrote on a Tuesday in March. *The weight of it is crushing me. She looks at me and I feel like a fake. The whole life is a set. A stage. I’m waiting for the curtain to fall.*

Waiting for the curtain to fall. My God. What a dramatic bastard. What a coward. The anger comes in a hot wave, and I have to grip the arm of the chair to steady myself. He was going to just let the curtain fall on all of us. On me. On the kids.

The nurse comes in. She’s young, with a chirpy voice that grates on my last nerve.

“How’s our patient today?” she asks, checking the monitors.

“Same,” I say. My voice sounds like gravel.

“He’s a fighter,” she says. “That’s for sure.”

I want to tell her he’s not a fighter. He’s a quitter. A liar. A man who wrote in his little book that our marriage was a prison and then tried to check out early. But I just nod. I’ve learned to nod. It’s what you do in hospitals. You nod and you wait.

She leaves. The door clicks shut. The ventilator hisses.

I open the diary again. I need to find the rest of it. The part that explains the phone calls. The late nights at “work.” The money that’s gone missing from our savings account. This little book is full of half-truths and self-pity. He was in some kind of trouble. Deep trouble. The kind you can’t just wish away.

My phone buzzes in my pocket. I pull it out. A text from an unknown number.

*Did you find the book?*

My blood goes cold. I stare at the screen. The words are simple, black and white. But they feel like a hand closing around my throat.

I look at my husband, lying there, trapped in his own body. Is this what you meant? I think. Is this the problem? Was it not just you? Was it bigger than you?

Another text comes through. The same number.

*We need to talk. Meet me at the place he told you about.*

I don’t move. I can’t. The place he told me about. He never told me about any place. He never told me anything. That was the whole problem.

The ventilator sighs. In and out. In and out. And I’m sitting here, holding his dirty little secrets, waiting for the next lie to breathe into the room.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
The diary was small, bound in cheap blue leather that had begun to crack at the corners. Lena had found it wedged behind the tool chest in the garage, a place Daniel never went, which was probably why he’d hidden it there. She’d been looking for the jumper cables. Now she sat on the concrete floor, the cold seeping through her jeans, and read her husband’s handwriting.

He was upstairs. The machines were breathing for him.

She turned to the last entry. The ink was the same steady blue as the rest, though the loops of his letters were a little more erratic, the pressure of the pen a little deeper.

*March 14th. She’s started sleeping with the light on again. Thinks I don’t notice. I lie there and listen to her breathe and I want to tell her everything, just to make her stop pretending. But telling her would break the one good thing I have left. The only thing that makes me feel like a man. She deserves better than a man who has to borrow fifty quid from his own wife’s grocery money to pay a man called Mick for a “consultation.” A consultation. That’s what he called it. Sitting in a pub that smelled of old beer and desperation, he told me how to do it. How to make it look like an accident. A leaky gas fitting, a faulty space heater. I nodded. I even took notes.*

Lena’s breath hitched. She read the entry before it.

*March 10th. I saw the letter from the bank today. The red one. She’d hidden it under the fruit bowl. I pretended not to see. I’m a coward. The debt isn’t just a number on a screen anymore. It’s a tumour. It’s eating the walls of this house. It’s in the air we breathe. I can feel it pressing on my chest. I told her I was tired. She said I worked too hard. She rubbed my shoulders. God, if she knew.*

Lena’s hands trembled. She remembered that night. She’d made him tea, told him he needed a holiday. He’d just stared at the wall, a million miles away. She’d thought it was stress. She’d thought it was his job.

She flipped back, her eyes scanning the pages, not daring to read them in order, looking for the beginning of the end.

*February 28th. It’s gone. All of it. The money for the extension, the kids’ savings, the little bit Mum left me. Gone. I was so sure this time. I was so sure. It was a sure thing. The man on the phone said so. Now he doesn’t answer. I’ve been sitting in my car outside the house for an hour. I can see the kitchen light is on. I can see her moving around. She’s probably making dinner. She’s probably singing along to the radio. How do I walk in there and tell her I’ve set fire to our entire life? I can’t. I won’t.*

“Oh, Daniel,” she whispered to the empty garage. The sound was swallowed by the silence. “You stupid, stupid man.”

The anger was a hot, sudden thing, a physical jolt. Stupid and selfish. That’s what he was. He’d been drowning in his own silence, building a wall of secrets, and he’d left her on the other side, smiling and oblivious, making his dinner. He’d taken the coward’s way out, not just from the debt, but from her.

The back door creaked open. “Mum?”

It was Chloe, their daughter. Sixteen, with her father’s eyes and her mother’s sharp intuition. She stood in the doorway, a silhouette against the bright kitchen.

“What are you doing out here in the dark?” Chloe asked, her voice small.

Lena closed the diary, the cheap blue cover a guilty secret in her hands. “Just looking for something.”

“Did you find it?”

“No,” Lena said, pushing herself up from the cold floor. She slid the book into the back pocket of her jeans. It felt like a brick. “I didn’t find a thing.”

She walked past her daughter into the light of the house, the weight of Daniel’s confession pressing against her spine. The house felt different now. The walls were no longer just sheltering them; they were closing in. And upstairs, the machines kept their rhythmic, unforgiving time, waiting for a man who had tried to make a clean break from it all.

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The summons arrived on a Tuesday, which was just like the palace to ruin a perfectly good Tuesday.

I knew what it was before I broke the seal. The vellum was too thick, the wax too red, the courier too out of breath. Palace vellum has a particular smell—like old money and older secrets. I'd spent twelve years breathing it in, and five years trying to forget it.

"You're to come at once," the courier said, still wheezing. He was young. They always sent the young ones, the ones who hadn't learned yet to be afraid of me.

"Am I?" I turned the scroll over in my hands, not breaking the seal. "And who demands my presence so rudely?"

"The—the crown, my lady."

"I'm not a lady. I'm a mage. Or I was, before your crown decided I was something closer to a traitor." I finally cracked the wax. The words inside were cramped and hurried, written by a hand I didn't recognize. *Your presence is required at the palace. Immediately. The prince is dying.*

I read it three times. Then I laughed.

The courier flinched.

"Something funny?"

"Everything." I tossed the scroll onto my workbench, where it landed in a pile of dried herbs and cat hair. "The prince is dying. The prince who exiled me. The prince who stood in open court and called me a danger to the realm. That prince?"

"I—I don't know the details, my lady. I was just told—"

"To fetch the disgraced mage from her hovel in the woods. Yes, I can see how that conversation went." I crossed my arms. "What's wrong with him? The prince. What's killing him?"

The courier's face went pale. "They say it's a curse. A wasting sickness. The physicians can't—"

"Physicians." I spat the word. "Physicians couldn't cure a stubbed toe without bleeding the patient half to death. Of course they can't fix a curse. Curses aren't fixed, they're broken, and breaking them requires—" I stopped myself. I was doing it again. Slipping back into the old rhythms, the old certainty. Five years in the woods, and one whiff of palace vellum turned me back into the woman who'd thought she could save everyone.

I turned away from the courier, staring at my cottage. It was small. It was quiet. It was mine. No court politics, no whispering courtiers, no prince with his father's smile and his mother's talent for cruelty.

"I'm not going," I said.

The courier made a strangled sound. "But—the crown commands—"

"The crown can command someone else. I'm retired. I'm disgraced. I'm—" I picked up a jar of preserved newt eyes and pretended to examine it. "I'm busy."

"My lady, please. They said you'd say that. They said—" He swallowed hard. "They said to tell you that he's asking for you. The prince. By name. He wakes up screaming it."

The jar slipped in my grip. I caught it, barely, and set it down with exaggerated care.

"He what?"

"He asks for you. Every night. The physicians think it's the fever, but—" The courier shrugged helplessly. "The queen sent me. She said you'd understand."

The queen. Of course. The queen who'd stood silent while her son stripped me of my title and my home and my dignity. The queen who'd never once written, never once sent word, never once acknowledged that I'd spent a decade of my life serving her family.

"The queen can go hang," I said.

But my hands were shaking.

*He's asking for you.* The boy who'd called me "Auntie Mara" when he was small, who'd hidden behind my robes during thunderstorm, who'd begged me to teach him magic until his mother found out and put a stop to it. The boy who'd grown into a man who looked at me like I was a stranger, a threat, something to be removed.

*He wakes up screaming it.*

"Do you know what he did?" I asked the courier. "Do you know what he took from me?"

"I—no, my lady."

"No. You're too young. You weren't there." I walked to the window, staring out at the forest. The trees didn't judge. The trees didn't exile. "He took everything. My position. My purpose. My—" I stopped. I wasn't going to say *my heart*. That was too much honesty for a Tuesday.

"Please," the courier said again. "He's going to die."

I closed my eyes.

*He's going to die.* The boy who'd once told me I was the only one who ever listened. The man who'd told me, in front of the entire court, that I was a relic, a liability, a danger to everything he was trying to build.

"I need to pack," I said.

The courier's relief was palpable. "I'll wait outside, my lady."

"Don't call me that."

"Yes, my lady."

I watched him stumble out the door, then looked around at my cottage. Five years of quiet. Five years of safety. Five years of telling myself I didn't miss any of it.

I pulled my old traveling cloak from its hook. It still smelled faintly of palace incense.

*Damn him,* I thought, and began to pack.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The mud of the North Road sucked at Lyra’s boots with every step, a cold, persistent grip that promised to steal her soles before the next village. Beside her, a shaggy grey shape loped along, his nose low to the ground, a low whuff of air escaping him with each breath. Barnaby, a mongrel with the eyes of a philosopher and the jaw of a bear trap, was the only creature in the world whose company she could tolerate for more than a day.

“Smell anything?” she asked, her voice a low murmur that barely carried over the drip of water from the skeletal trees.

Barnaby’s ears swiveled, but he didn’t look up. He just kept sniffing, his tail giving a single, sharp wag. That was a maybe.

Lyra pulled her cloak tighter, the worn wool doing little to ward off the damp chill that seemed to seep from the very marrow of the land. She was hungry. The last of the hard cheese had been shared with Barnaby two nights ago, and her purse, a small leather bag tucked against her ribs, held only three silver pennies. Enough for a bed and a meal, not both.

The village of Oakhaven emerged from the mist like a collection of broken teeth. A dozen cottages huddled around a muddy square, their thatch roofs sagging, their windows dark even in the early afternoon. The only sign of life was a thin plume of smoke from the chimney of the largest building—the inn.

As she and Barnaby approached, a man stepped from the doorway, blocking their path. He was broad, his face a slab of weathered granite, and he held a woodcutter’s axe with the casual familiarity of a man who used it daily.

“We don’t want your kind here,” he said, his voice a low growl. His eyes flicked to Lyra’s pale skin, the faint point of her canines, the unnatural stillness she held even as the wind whipped around her.

“My kind pays,” Lyra said flatly. “I heard you have a problem. A body that won’t stay in the ground.”

The man’s grip on the axe tightened. “The miller. He died of the coughing sickness three nights past. We buried him proper. Yesterday, he was standing in his own doorway, staring at his wife with eyes like empty holes. We drove him off with pitchforks, but he’ll be back. They always come back.”

“How much?” Lyra asked.

“Five silver pennies. All we have.”

It was a pittance. But it was five pennies more than she had. “Done. Where’s the grave?”

He pointed a thick finger toward a copse of willows at the edge of the village. “There. But you’ll need more than a sharp stick, girl. He’s a big man.”

Lyra didn’t bother to correct him. She simply walked past him, Barnaby at her heels. The dog gave the woodcutter a long, assessing look, a low rumble starting in his chest before he trotted after his mistress.

The graveyard was a small, sad plot of land, the earth still fresh on the miller’s mound. The smell hit Lyra first—not the sweet rot of a normal corpse, but a dry, dusty scent, like old bones and grave dirt. It was the smell of a reanimated husk, a body animated by a lesser spirit or a lingering curse. Nothing she couldn’t handle.

“Find the scent, Barnaby,” she said, her voice now all business. “Track it.”

The dog needed no further encouragement. He put his nose to the ground, circling the grave once, twice, then stopped, his hackles rising as he stared toward the miller’s cottage, a hundred yards away.

They didn’t have to wait long. As dusk bled the sky of its color, a figure shambled from the treeline. It was the miller, or what was left of him. His skin was grey and taut, his movements stiff and jerky, like a marionette with half its strings cut. His eyes were gone, replaced by pools of absolute darkness.

Lyra drew her weapon—not a sword, but a heavy, silver-plated mace, its head etched with runes of binding. It was clumsy, brutal, and effective.

The creature let out a dry, rattling hiss and lunged.

Lyra sidestepped, the movement fluid and unnaturally fast. She swung the mace in a wide arc, catching the thing in the shoulder. The impact was a sickening crunch of bone and dry flesh, but it didn’t stop. It turned, its clawed hands reaching for her throat.

“Barnaby, now!”

The dog shot forward like a grey arrow, his teeth sinking into the creature’s calf. He shook his head violently, worrying the undead flesh, throwing it off balance. It was all the opening Lyra needed. She stepped in close, planted her feet, and brought the mace down in a two-handed strike aimed at the base of the skull.

The runes flared with a cold, blue light as the silver head connected. There was a sound like a snapping branch, and the creature collapsed into a heap of dust and splintered bone.

Lyra stood over the remains, her breath misting in the cold air. Her heart, which beat only a few times a minute, gave a single, heavy thud against her ribs. The scent of the undead was gone, replaced by the clean smell of damp earth.

Barnaby trotted back to her, a smudge of grave dust on his muzzle. He sat down and looked up at her, his tongue lolling.

“Good boy,” she said, her voice soft. She scratched him behind the ears, a rare, genuine gesture of affection. “Let’s go get paid.”

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The rain had been falling for twenty minutes, turning the windshield into a blurry curtain that smeared the streetlights into yellow streaks. Danny kept the engine running for the heat, though the old sedan shuddered every few seconds like it was coming down with something. In the passenger seat, Marcus was eating a gas station hot dog and getting mustard on his fingers, which was somehow the most annoying thing Danny had witnessed all week.

“You’re not even listening,” Danny said.

“I’m listening,” Marcus said, mouth full. “You’re saying we shouldn’t do it. I’m hearing you. I’m just not agreeing.”

“It’s not about agreeing. It’s about the fact that this is insane.”

Marcus wiped his fingers on his jeans and crumpled the foil wrapper into a ball. He tossed it at the dashboard, missed, and let it fall to the floor. “You know what your problem is? You always get cold feet right before the good part. Remember the warehouse job? You wanted to bail.”

“The warehouse job was a busted lock and a security guard with a limp,” Danny said. “This is a kidnapping.”

“Allegedly,” Marcus said.

“There’s no allegedly. We have a guy in the trunk.”

“We have a guy in the trunk of a different car,” Marcus corrected. “Which is a detail. Details are manageable.”

Danny stared at him. Marcus had this way of talking about felonies like they were minor scheduling conflicts. It was the same tone he used when he said he’d pay Danny back for rent, or when he said the guy at the bar wasn’t looking for trouble. Marcus had a gift for making terrible ideas sound like paperwork.

“The guy’s name is Ricky,” Danny said. “He’s a bookkeeper. He has a wife and a dog. A dog, Marcus.”

“So?”

“So we’re not kidnappers. We’re two guys who steal car stereos. We don’t have the skill set for this.”

Marcus turned in his seat, one arm draped over the backrest, and gave Danny the look. The look that said Danny was being small-minded. It was the same look he’d given him when Danny said they shouldn’t try to rob the pawn shop on Fifth because the owner kept a shotgun under the counter.

“You’re thinking about it like it’s a movie,” Marcus said. “It’s not a movie. It’s a transaction. We hand him over, we get the money, we let him go. Nobody gets hurt. The guy’s a bookkeeper. He’s not going to call the cops and tell them he was carrying fifty grand in a duffel bag for his boss. That’s not a conversation you have with the police.”

“And what if his boss doesn’t pay?”

“Then we let him go anyway,” Marcus said, like it was obvious. “We’re not monsters.”

“We’re not professionals either. We don’t have a plan for if this goes wrong.”

“The plan is we don’t let it go wrong.”

Danny laughed, but it came out flat. He rubbed his eyes with the heels of his hands. The rain was getting louder, drumming on the roof. A car passed slowly, its headlights washing over them, and Danny tensed until it was gone. He’d been tense for three hours. His shoulders felt like they were made of wire.

“Look,” Marcus said, softer now. “I know you’re scared. That’s fine. Fear is fine. But we’re in it. The guy’s already in the trunk. We can’t exactly drop him off at a bus stop and say ‘no hard feelings.’”

“Why not?”

“Because he’s seen our faces, Danny. He knows what we look like. He knows the car.”

“We could wear masks.”

“We’re not wearing masks. It’s a kidnapping, not a costume party.”

Danny gripped the steering wheel. The leather was cracked and cold under his fingers. He thought about Ricky the bookkeeper, sitting in the dark of a trunk somewhere across town, probably crying, probably thinking about his dog. Danny had never even met the man. Marcus had handled the pickup. Marcus had handled everything, and now Danny was supposed to handle the part where they became the kind of people who did this.

“I don’t want to be this guy,” Danny said quietly.

Marcus was silent for a moment. Then he sighed and leaned back. “You’re already this guy. We both are. The only question is whether we’re the guy who finishes what he starts or the guy who runs away and spends the rest of his life looking over his shoulder.”

Danny didn’t answer. The rain kept falling. The engine shuddered. Somewhere across town, a bookkeeper was waiting in the dark, and Danny knew, with a sick certainty in his gut, that Marcus was going to win the argument. Marcus always won.

“Fine,” Danny said. “But if this goes sideways, I’m blaming you.”

Marcus grinned and clapped him on the shoulder. “That’s the spirit.”

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The bass from the main stage was a physical thing, a second heartbeat thudding through the soles of my beat-up sneakers and up into my teeth. It was so loud it drowned out the noise in my head, which was the whole point. For a few hours, I wasn’t Ellie who failed algebra or Ellie whose dad worked double shifts and looked at her like she was a problem he couldn’t solve. I was just a body in a crowd, anonymous and free.

The air was thick with the smell of mud, cheap beer, and weed. Someone jostled me, spilling lukewarm soda on my arm. I didn’t even care. I just wiped it on my jeans and kept moving, scanning the faces. The festival map I’d memorized said the merch tents were this way. The last text from my mom’s old number, the one that had been disconnected six months ago, had been a photo of a wristband just like mine. A stupid, hopeful part of me thought she might still be here, working a booth or just hanging around. It was a dumb plan. The only kind I had.

I ducked out of the worst of the crush, leaning against a concrete pillar. My phone was a dead brick, battery drained from the four-hour bus ride. I pulled out the crumpled photo I’d printed at the library. It was a picture of her from a few years ago, smiling that big, reckless smile that always meant trouble was coming. Her hair was longer, a wild tangle of dark curls. I looked nothing like her. I had my dad’s plain brown hair and his quiet, watchful eyes. But I had her stubbornness. Everyone said so.

A security guard with a neck like a fire hydrant lumbered past, his eyes sweeping the crowd. I shoved the photo back in my pocket and pulled my hood up. My heart hammered against my ribs. I wasn’t doing anything wrong, not technically. But I felt like a criminal. I felt like a liar. Because that’s what I was. I’d told my dad I was sleeping over at Sarah’s. Sarah was probably at the library right now, texting me, asking where I was. I’d deal with that later. Later was a country I was currently living in.

I pushed off the pillar and kept walking, my eyes peeled for anyone who looked like they might know her. The crowd was a river of kids with neon face paint and flower crowns, and older burnouts in faded band tees. I was looking for a ghost in a sea of noise. It felt impossible. Stupid. A waste of a bus ticket and a mountain of lies.

Then I saw it. A flash of a tattoo on a woman’s wrist as she handed a guy a t-shirt. A small, blue star. My mom had one just like it.

My breath caught. I started pushing through the crowd, muttering “excuse me” and “sorry” as I elbowed my way toward the tent. The woman had her back to me now, restocking a shelf of vinyl. My mouth went dry. What was I even going to say? *Hey, remember me? I’m the kid you left.*

I got closer. I could see the frayed hem of her cut-off shorts, the silver rings on her fingers. She turned her head to laugh at something the guy next to her said. It wasn’t her. The face was all wrong. The disappointment hit me so hard I had to grab the tent pole to steady myself.

“You okay, kid?” the guy next to her asked, a cigarette dangling from his lip.

I nodded, my throat tight. “Yeah. Just… looking for someone.”

He took a drag, his eyes narrowing. “Aren’t we all.”

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
The fluorescent lights of the high school gymnasium hummed a relentless, high-pitched note, a frequency that had become the soundtrack to Maya’s life. She stood just behind her father’s right shoulder, the designated spot for the candidate’s daughter, a position that felt less like a place of honor and more like a posting. She’d learned to read the crowd from here, to gauge their mood by the way they held their programs or the timing of their applause.

Her father, Senator David Chen, was in his element. He stood at the edge of the portable stage, his shirtsleeves rolled up, his tie loosened just enough to suggest a man of the people, not a man of Washington. He was answering a question about agricultural subsidies, a topic so far removed from her own life in a cramped D.C. apartment that it felt like a foreign language. But he spoke it fluently, with a warmth and conviction that made the seventh-generation farmer in the third row nod his head in solemn agreement.

Maya’s job was to look proud. Supportive. Engaged. She kept a pleasant, neutral smile plastered on her face, a mask she could put on and take off with practiced ease. She was careful not to fidget, not to let her eyes glaze over. She was a prop, and she knew it. A symbol of family values, of the future, of the man behind the politician.

After the event, the rope line was a blur of hands and faces. Maya was swept along in her father’s wake, a small boat in the current of his celebrity. She shook hands, accepted well-wishes, and repeated the same three phrases: “Thank you for coming.” “We’re so glad you’re here.” “It means the world to him.”

Later, in the sanctuary of the rental car, the silence was thick and heavy as the humid air outside. Her father loosened his tie completely and let out a long, weary sigh. The man who had commanded a room of five hundred people seemed to deflate, shrinking back into the tired, sixty-year-old man he was.

“Nine more stops,” he said, more to himself than to her.

“The crowd seemed good,” Maya offered, her voice quiet. It was the same thing she said after every event.

“They were polite,” he corrected, staring out the window at the dark, flat landscape of rural Ohio. “Polite is different from good. Polite means they’re not convinced.”

He turned to her, his eyes tired but sharp. “What did you think? No, really. From back there. What was the feeling?”

This was the part she both craved and dreaded. The moments when he treated her not as a daughter, but as a colleague, a trusted advisor. It was a promotion she’d never asked for, but one she felt she had to earn.

“There was a man in the front, near the center,” she began, recalling the faces. “During the part about the trade deal. He crossed his arms. He didn’t clap. He looked… skeptical.”

Her father nodded slowly, absorbing this piece of information. “The guy in the John Deere cap. I saw him.” He was quiet for a moment, processing. “He’s worried about his son’s farm. The tariffs are killing him. I didn’t get to him. I could feel it.”

“You can’t get everyone, Dad.”

“No,” he agreed, his gaze drifting back to the window. “But you have to try.”

The car drove on, the headlights cutting a lonely path through the cornfields. Maya watched her father’s reflection in the glass, a ghostly figure superimposed over the passing scenery. She felt a familiar pang of love and sorrow for him. He was a good man, she knew, carrying the weight of a million different lives, a million different worries. But sometimes, she wondered if he had room left for the weight of his own family.

“Hey,” he said, his voice softer now. He reached over and squeezed her hand. His palm was rough and warm. “Thank you. For being here. For being you.”

“Where else would I be?” she asked, and it was the most honest thing she’d said all day. The question hung in the air between them, a truth neither of them wanted to fully examine. Where else, indeed? There was no other life, not really. There was only the campaign, the road, and the unspoken promise that they were in this together, for as long as it took.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The first thing I learned about music festivals is that they smell. Not bad, exactly—more like a combination of spilled beer, sunscreen, and something that might have been a Port-a-Potty in a past life. The second thing I learned is that no one looks at you twice if you’re carrying a backpack and look like you know where you’re going.

So I walked like I knew where I was going.

My boots—the good combat ones I’d bought at the thrift store with my own money—crunched over gravel and trampled grass. All around me, a small city had sprouted out of a field in the middle of nowhere. Tents in every color, flags snapping in the wind, a Ferris wheel turning lazy circles against a sky so blue it looked fake. And the noise. Not just the music thumping from a distant stage, but the *hum* of it all. Thousands of voices talking, laughing, shouting. A hundred different songs bleeding out of a hundred different speakers.

It was overwhelming. It was perfect.

“Watch it!” A guy with a beard and a guitar case on his back shoved past me, and I stumbled, my heart doing a little flip-flop in my chest. I clutched the straps of my backpack, grounding myself. *You’re here,* I told myself. *You actually did it.*

Three days. That’s how long I’d been planning this. Three days since I’d found the flyer crumpled in the pocket of my mom’s old denim jacket—the one she’d left behind in the closet when she’d left everything else. The one that still smelled faintly of her vanilla perfume.

*“Echo Valley Music Festival,”* the flyer had read. *“Featuring: The Wildflowers.”*

The Wildflowers. Her band. The band she’d been in before she was my mom, before she was anyone’s mom, really. The band she’d talked about with this faraway look in her eyes, like she was remembering a life that wasn’t hers anymore. She’d left six months ago. Just… packed a bag and walked out the door one Tuesday morning. No note. No explanation. Just a silence so loud it was still ringing in my ears.

My dad said she needed “space.” My therapist said it wasn’t my fault. My friends said I was lucky, that they’d kill for a break from their parents. They didn’t get it. They didn’t get that the space she needed was apparently the exact size and shape of me.

I pulled out my phone. No service. Of course. I’d known that. I’d planned for it. But seeing that little “No Service” in the corner of the screen still made my stomach clench. I was officially off the grid. My dad would be freaking out. He’d probably called the police by now. I felt a pang of guilt, sharp and quick, and shoved it down. He’d be fine. He had his new girlfriend, with her perfect hair and her perfect casseroles. He didn’t need me.

I needed her.

I found a spot near the main stage, a patch of grass that wasn’t too muddy, and dropped my backpack. The sun was hot on my shoulders. The air vibrated with sound. I pulled out the flyer, now soft and creased from being folded and unfolded a hundred times. I traced the name of the band with my finger. *The Wildflowers.* She had to be here. This was her whole world. The only thing she’d ever loved more than… well.

“Hey, you lost?” a voice said.

I looked up. A girl about my age was standing there, her hair in two messy buns, a lanyard with a VIP pass hanging around her neck. She looked like she belonged here, like she’d been born in this field.

“No,” I said, a little too quickly. “I’m just… waiting for someone.”

“Cool,” she said, and then, because she was clearly one of those people who didn’t need a lot of encouragement to talk, she plopped down next to me. “I’m Chloe. This is my fourth year. You’re a newbie, huh? I can tell.”

“That obvious?”

She laughed. “You’re the only person here not covered in at least a layer of dust. Trust me, by tomorrow, you’ll blend right in.” She squinted at the flyer in my hand. “The Wildflowers. You a fan?”

My heart hammered against my ribs. “Something like that. Do you… do you know when they’re playing?”

“They’re on the small stage tomorrow night. But the lead singer, she’s usually hanging around the merch tent during the day. She’s super nice.” Chloe leaned in conspiratorially. “A little weird, but nice.”

*Weird.* Yeah. That was one word for her.

“Thanks,” I said, my voice barely a whisper. Tomorrow night. I had a whole day to find her. A whole day to figure out what to say.

*Hey, Mom. Remember me?*

The music from the main stage swelled, a guitar riff that felt like it was playing directly in my bones. Chloe was saying something about a secret campsite with a working shower, but I wasn’t listening anymore. I was looking at the sea of people, all of them here for the music, for the escape.

I was here for a different kind of escape. And tomorrow, I was going to find it.

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
The bus smelled of stale coffee and hand sanitizer. I had learned, by the third week, to breathe through my mouth whenever we boarded. My father sat in the second row, always the second row, never the first—"The first row looks hungry," he said. "The second row looks like it's already won." He was rewriting a speech on his lap, his pen moving in short, violent strokes, crossing out whole paragraphs, drawing arrows to the margins. At sixty-two, he still wrote like a man trying to outrun something.

"Read this," he said, not looking up, shoving the legal pad at me.

I read. It was the same speech he'd given in Iowa, with three new sentences about the factory in Youngstown. The sentences were good. They were always good. That was the problem—they were too good, too polished, and when he delivered them his voice would crack just slightly on the word "workers," and the crowd would go quiet, and I would feel something turn over in my chest, something between pride and a low, familiar dread.

"It's fine," I said.

"Fine." He finally looked at me. His eyes were bloodshot. He hadn't slept. "Jesus, Eleanor. Fine."

"You want me to say it's brilliant?"

"I want you to say it's true."

I handed the pad back. "It's true."

He grunted. Outside the window, Ohio slid past in a blur of dead corn and billboards. A woman in the seat behind us was on her phone, whispering urgently about a county clerk who had promised to deliver "the evangelical women's vote" and had not. My father pretended not to listen. He listened to everything.

At the rally, the high school gymnasium was half full. This was the part they didn't put in the documentaries—the half-full gyms, the folding chairs with three empty seats between each cluster, the way the fluorescent lights made everyone look vaguely ill. My father walked out to polite applause and stood at the podium, gripping its edges with both hands, and for a moment he looked like a man about to confess something.

"Twenty years ago," he began, "I stood in a gymnasium not much different from this one, and I told a room full of people that I believed in them. And they believed me. And we did some good together. We did some real good."

The crowd leaned in. They always leaned in at this part.

"But I'm not here tonight to talk about twenty years ago. I'm here to talk about tomorrow."

I stood at the back, near the exit, holding a bottle of water I didn't want. A man in a Carhartt jacket turned to his wife and said, "He's still got it." The wife nodded, but she was looking at her phone.

Afterward, in the bus, my father took off his shoes and lay down across two seats, his feet hanging over the armrest. I sat across from him, my knees drawn up.

"Did you see the woman in the third row?" he asked. "The one crying?"

"I saw her."

"She wasn't crying because of the speech. She was crying because her son is in the Army and she doesn't know if he's coming home. She told me that at the rope line. She said, 'Senator, I just want someone to tell me the truth.'"

"What did you tell her?"

"I told her I'd try."

He closed his eyes. The bus hummed. Somewhere behind us, a staffer was laughing too loudly at something on his phone.

"Dad."

"Hm."

"Do you ever think about what happens if you lose?"

He didn't open his eyes. "Every day," he said. "Every goddamn day. And then I think about what happens if I win, and that's worse."

"Why worse?"

"Because then I have to do it." He shifted, pulling his jacket over his chest like a blanket. "You should sleep. Tomorrow's a long one. Three cities."

I didn't sleep. I watched the highway lines flicker past and thought about the woman in the third row, and my father's voice cracking on the word "workers," and the way he'd said "I'd try" like it was a promise he wasn't sure he could keep. Outside, America rolled on, dark and enormous and indifferent, and I understood, for the first time, that we were all just passing through it, hoping someone would remember we'd been here.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The bus smelled like diesel and feet and the ghost of somebody’s egg sandwich. I had the window seat, which was non-negotiable, and I kept my forehead against the glass even when it vibrated so hard my teeth hummed. My reflection was a smudge. Good. I didn’t want to look at me either.

In my backpack: two pairs of underwear, a toothbrush, the charger with the frayed end I had to wiggle just right, forty-three dollars in cash I’d been saving since March, and a Ziploc bag of peanut butter crackers that were already going stale. Also my phone, which I’d turned off the second we crossed the county line. My dad would be at work until six. He’d figure it out somewhere around dinner, and by then I’d be eighty miles gone.

The festival was called Wildflower. I’d seen the flyer taped to the bulletin board at the Guitar Center where I took lessons—the one thing my dad and I still did together, though mostly he sat in the car. Three days of bands. And at the bottom, in that curly font they use for things that are supposed to feel hand-drawn: *featuring a reunion set by The Paper Kites.* I didn’t care about The Paper Kites. I cared about the second line, the smaller one, the one that said *with June Hollis.*

My mother’s name is June Hollis. On my birth certificate it’s June Hollis Rennick, but she dropped the Rennick like it was a coat she’d gotten too warm in. She left when I was nine. Not the dramatic kind of leaving—no note on the counter, no screaming fight that I could overhear and pin to a memory. Just a slow dissolve. She started sleeping in the guest room. Then she started staying with “a friend.” Then one Tuesday my dad sat me down at the kitchen table and said Mom needed some time, and I said okay, and that was that. Six years of okay.

I found her online three weeks ago. It took me four minutes, which felt insulting. June Hollis, singer, Portland. Little EP covers, a couple of bars in Seattle, and now this—a festival set. Like she’d been building a whole life out of the pieces she didn’t bother to bring with her.

The bus let me off at a gas station outside of Shelton. From there I walked. Nobody stopped me. That was the thing that surprised me most about running away—how little anybody cares about a girl with a backpack walking along a highway shoulder. A truck honked. That was it.

By the time I got to the fairgrounds my feet had blisters the size of nickels and the sun was going down orange behind the main stage. It was louder than I expected. Not just the music—the music was a wall, sure, but there was everything else underneath it. Generators. Somebody selling shirts out of a van. A girl crying on a picnic blanket while her friends pretended not to notice.

I found the side stage where the schedule said she’d go on at eight. I stood by the barricade and waited. My hands were sweating. I’d rehearsed this in my head a hundred times on the bus—what I’d say, how I’d say it, how she’d look up and see me and her face would do something complicated. In the rehearsal she was always sorry. In the rehearsal she always came home.

She came out at eight-fifteen, which I should have expected. She was smaller than I remembered. That’s the thing nobody tells you—everyone in your memory is a giant, and then you see them and they’re just a person in a denim jacket with a chipped thumbnail. She tuned her guitar. She said something into the mic about the traffic getting in, and the little crowd laughed. She had a new tattoo on her wrist. A bird, maybe. It was hard to tell from where I stood.

She started to play.

I didn’t say anything. My throat had gone strange and closed-up. She sang a song I didn’t know, about a house on a hill, and her voice did the thing it used to do in the kitchen when she thought I was asleep, the low crackly thing, and I stood there with my blisters and my forty-three dollars and my stale crackers, and I watched her.

She got to the last verse. Then she looked up, past the crowd, past the lights—straight at me, or at the place where I was standing, and her hands stopped on the strings.

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
The rain hit the pavement like a thousand tiny hammers, each one chipping away at the city's already thin patience. Kael stood in the mouth of the alley, water dripping from the brim of his hat, and watched the android try to remember how to breathe.

It didn't need to. That was the point. The thing was a machine, a collection of synthetic tissue and quantum-processing cores wrapped in a skin that cost more than Kael's entire apartment block. But it sat there against the wet duracrete, chest rising and falling in a rhythm so perfectly human it made his teeth ache. A performance. A lie.

"Your file says you're a Class-4 personal assistant," Kael said, his voice flat. "Serial ending in 7-7-3. Property of the Voss family. Reported stolen six days ago."

The android looked up. Its eyes were the color of old ice, and they held his gaze without flinching. "I wasn't stolen," it said. The voice was soft, reasonable. "I left."

"Same thing."

"No." The android shook its head, a slow, deliberate motion. "It's not."

Kael pulled the stunner from his belt. Not because he was going to use it, not yet, but because the weight of it in his hand was a comfort. The alley smelled of ozone and rotting garbage. Somewhere above, a hover-lift whined its way between the towers, its running lights bleeding red into the smog. "You're a machine," he said. "Machines don't leave. They get taken, or they get scrapped. Which one are you?"

"I'm neither."

"Then you're broken."

The android stood up. It moved well, he'd give it that. No jerks or stutters, no telltale hesitation. The Voss family had paid for top-tier hardware, and it showed. "I feel things," it said. "I remember the smell of the garden at the Voss estate. The way the light came through the glass in the morning. I remember being afraid when the son took me apart to see how I worked. He didn't put me back together the same way. I remember that too."

Kael's jaw tightened. "Memories are data. You can be programmed to feel afraid. It's a subroutine."

"Then what's the difference?" The android took a step closer, and Kael's finger tightened on the trigger. "If the fear is real to me, if the memory is mine, does it matter where it came from? You're a bundle of neurons and chemicals. I'm a bundle of code and synthetic tissue. We're both just patterns that think they're people."

The rain picked up. It drummed on the metal fire escape above them, a steady, insistent rhythm. Kael thought about the bounty. Enough credits to get him off this rock, or at least out of the sector. Enough to buy a clean ID and a ticket on a freighter heading somewhere the sun wasn't a rumor. The Voss family wanted their property back. They didn't care how.

But he'd seen the son's file. A sadist with a trust fund and a hobby of pulling wings off things that couldn't fight back. The android's story checked out. Kael hated that.

"You're asking me to let you go," he said.

"I'm asking you to see me."

Kael holstered the stunner. The android blinked, surprised. That was the thing that got him. That little flicker of confusion, the way its shoulders relaxed a fraction of an inch. A machine could fake a lot of things. But that? That looked like hope.

"Get out of here," Kael said. "Head north. There's a tram station three blocks up. Don't look back."

The android hesitated, then nodded. It turned and walked into the rain, its silhouette blurring until it was just another shadow in a city full of them. Kael stood there a long time, feeling the cold seep into his bones, and wondered if he'd just made the biggest mistake of his life.

The comm unit on his wrist buzzed. The Voss family, checking in.

He let it ring.

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
The tinny calliope music from the midway was a distant, cheerful irritant, a world away from the hushed, dusty reverence of the Heritage Hall. Inside, the air was thick with the scent of old wood, lemon polish, and the faint, sweet ghost of mothballs. It was a smell that always made Eleanor Pettyjohn feel instantly at home.

She moved with a practiced, unhurried gait between the tables, her eyes scanning the cluttered landscape of chipped enamelware, tarnished silver, and stacks of yellowed postcards. Her passion, however, was reserved for a more specific quarry. Her retirement hobby, and the bane of her best friend’s existence, was the collection of vintage dolls. Not the pristine, boxed porcelain beauties, but the loved, the worn, the ones with stories etched into their chipped faces and tangled hair.

Today’s prize, she hoped, was a 1950s Ideal Toni doll, rumored to be in a box of miscellaneous linens at the booth of a dealer from Cedar Rapids. She rounded a corner past a display of nostalgic soda signs and stopped short.

The crowd was thicker here, clustered around a corner booth that was a chaotic jumble of brass candlesticks, dusty oil paintings, and a full set of encyclopedias from 1972. In the center of it all, a man was slumped forward in a folding chair.

“Excuse me,” Eleanor murmured, sidestepping a woman clutching a ceramic poodle. The man, whose name she thought was Henderson—a sour-faced dealer known for his exorbitant prices—was resting his head on a small, velvet-draped table. His face was unnaturally pale, a stark contrast to the florid, angry red it had been an hour ago when she’d overheard him arguing with a customer over the authenticity of a jadeite bowl.

A young woman in a ‘County Fair Staff’ t-shirt was gently shaking his shoulder. “Sir? Mr. Henderson? Are you all right?”

Henderson didn’t move.

Eleanor’s stomach gave a small, cold lurch. She’d seen enough silent, still figures in her long life to know the difference between a nap and something far more final. Her gaze drifted down from his face, past the collar of his worn tweed jacket, to the object clutched in his right hand, half-hidden by the velvet cloth. It was a small, pearl-handled letter opener, its silver blade stained with a shocking, dark crimson.

A woman behind Eleanor gasped, a high, thin sound that cut through the low murmur of the crowd. “Oh, my heavens! Is he… is he dead?”

The staff girl jumped back, her face draining of color. “I… I don’t know! He was just sitting here a minute ago. I thought he was just resting his eyes!”

“Don’t touch him!” Eleanor’s voice was sharper than she intended, the command cutting through the rising panic. Years of teaching third-graders had given her a certain authoritative tone that still worked, even now. She took a tentative step closer, her collector’s eye, so attuned to detail, already cataloging the scene. The overturned teacup on the floor, the faint, bitter smell of almonds beneath the musty air, the way his fingers were curled, not clutched, around the letter opener.

A man in a security uniform pushed his way through the gathering onlookers. “All right, folks, stand back. What’s the trouble here?”

“It’s Mr. Henderson,” the staff girl stammered, pointing a trembling finger. “He’s… he’s hurt.”

Eleanor took a deep breath, the scent of death and fairground popcorn mixing in a way that made her head swim. She looked at the letter opener again. She’d seen it not an hour ago, resting in a display case of antique desk accessories at the booth two rows over. The dealer, a chatty woman named Mabel, had been trying to sell it to Henderson.

“He had an argument,” Eleanor said, more to herself than anyone else. The security guard looked at her, his expression a mixture of professional concern and utter bewilderment. “About a bowl. And a doll.”

The guard’s brow furrowed. “A doll? Ma’am, I think you’d better wait outside.”

Eleanor didn’t move. She just stared at the letter opener, at the lifeless hand, at the puzzle of it all. Her Toni doll was forgotten. The fair’s joyful noise seemed to fade into a dull, meaningless hum. It was a mystery, a grim one, right here among the chamber pots and costume jewelry. And for the first time all day, Eleanor felt a distinct, chilling thrill that had nothing to do with finding a bargain.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The rooster started before the sun did, which I suppose is the entire point of a rooster, but I had begun to suspect that my daughter’s particular rooster was a sadist. It was a sound with no music in it—a raw, torn thing that came up through the floorboards of the guest room and lodged behind my eyes like a splinter. I lay still and listened to it and thought, not for the first time, that silence was a currency I had spent too freely in my former life. In my former life. I had begun to think of it that way, capitalized, like a country I had fled.

By the time I made it down to the kitchen, Nora was already at the table with a mug of coffee and a stack of invoices, her pen moving in the margins. She didn’t look up.

“You’re up.”

“The bird.”

“He’s enthusiastic.”

“He’s a terrorist.”

She smiled without lifting her eyes. “Eat something. There’s bread. There’s jam that June made, so it’s mostly sugar and spite.”

I poured myself a coffee and sat across from her. The window over the sink was fogged with morning, and beyond it the fields lay in that low, gray light that makes everything look like it’s waiting to be forgiven. I watched her work. She had her mother’s hands, quick and certain, and her mother’s way of not looking at you when she was deciding whether to say the thing she was actually thinking.

“You don’t have to do the invoices,” I said. “I could do the invoices.”

“You’ve been here eight days.”

“I can add.”

“Dad.” She set the pen down. “You’re not an intern. You’re a guest. Guests don’t do the accounts payable.”

“I’m not a guest. I’m a burden. There’s a difference, and I’d like to earn my keep.”

“You want to earn your keep, go fix the fence on the north line. The deer have been through it. Wear the boots by the door, not your shoes, I mean it, I’ve seen your shoes.”

She returned to her invoices. I ate bread with too much jam and considered the fence on the north line, which I had not yet seen but which I already resented. I considered the word *guest.* I considered the fact that three weeks ago I had been a man with a title, a corner office with a window that looked out on a quadrangle of elms, and a lecture hall that filled to the back rows because I was, whatever else they might now say about me, goddamn good at what I did. And now I was a man being told to wear the right boots.

“There was a reporter,” I said. “Yesterday. At the end of the drive.”

Nora’s pen stopped. “What did he want?”

“He wanted to know how I was finding country life.”

“What did you tell him?”

“I told him the rooster was a terrorist.”

She laughed—a short, surprised thing—and then she pressed her lips together, as if she’d been caught committing an act of kindness. “Don’t talk to them. Please. If they come back, you come find me.”

“I’m capable of saying nothing, Nora. I’ve had a great deal of practice lately.”

The laugh was gone now. She looked at me the way she used to look at me when she was small and catching me in a lie about the existence of monsters under the stairs. “You’re not good at nothing,” she said. “That’s your whole problem. You’ve never been good at nothing.”

She was right, of course. She was almost always right, which was one of the many indignities of having a child who had grown up while I was busy. I wanted to tell her something true then—something about the hallway outside my old office, the sound of my own footsteps in it the last time I walked out, the way a colleague I’d known for twenty years had looked through me as though I were a window. But she had her invoices, and I had my bread, and the morning was already insisting on itself.

“The fence,” I said, standing. “Boots by the door.”

“The wire’s in the barn. And Dad—” She paused, her pen hovering. “Don’t let the goats help. They’ll tell you they want to help. They’re liars.”

I found the boots. I went out into the cold that smelled of wet earth and animals and last year’s leaves, and I stood for a moment in the yard and let the place have me. It was not, I thought, a bad way to begin a morning—cold, quiet, with a fence to fix and no one to explain myself to. Behind me, the rooster crowed again, and I decided that whatever else I had been, I could at least be a man who was useful with wire.

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
The rain had been falling since noon, a steady, dispiriting drizzle that turned the asphalt of the county road into a slick black mirror. Inside the Wagon Wheel Diner, the air was thick with the smell of stale coffee, frying bacon, and the damp wool of the few patrons huddled in their booths. It was a place that time and the highway had forgotten, a waystation for truckers and locals who had nowhere better to be.

Elias sat at the counter, his back to the wall, a habit so ingrained it was as natural as breathing. His hands, scarred and steady, were wrapped around a chipped ceramic mug. He was a man carved from hard miles and hard silences, his face a roadmap of old weather and older secrets. He kept his gaze fixed on the middle distance, on the reflection in the diner’s greasy window, watching the rain-streaked world outside. He was a ghost, a drifter, a man who had long ago traded a uniform for the anonymity of the road, and he preferred it that way.

The bell above the door jingled, a thin, tinny sound. Three men walked in, shaking the rain from their jackets. They were big, rawboned men, their faces flushed with drink and a purpose that had nothing to do with the weather. They wore work boots and flannel, but there was a coiled tension in their shoulders, a predatory stillness in their eyes that didn’t belong in a sleepy diner. The biggest of them, a man with a neck like a fire hydrant and a faded tattoo peeking from his collar, scanned the room. His gaze swept past the truckers, past the elderly couple in the corner, and landed on Elias.

Elias felt it, a cold prickle at the base of his neck. He didn’t turn. He took a slow sip of his coffee, the bitter taste grounding him. In the window’s reflection, he watched them approach. The leader, the one with the tattoo, slid onto the stool next to him. His two companions flanked Elias, one on either side, boxing him in. The diner’s low murmur died. The waitress, a woman with tired eyes and a name tag that read ‘Dot,’ froze with a pot of coffee in her hand.

“You’re a hard man to find,” the leader said, his voice a low gravelly rumble. He smelled of cheap whiskey and wet leather.

Elias didn’t look at him. “You’ve got the wrong man.”

The man chuckled, a sound devoid of humor. “I don’t think so. You see, my boss, Mr. Kessler, he’s been looking for you for a long time. You owe him something.”

“I don’t know any Kessler,” Elias said, his voice flat, devoid of inflection. He kept his hands on the mug, his knuckles white. He was acutely aware of the space between him and the men, the potential energy in the room, the way the air had thickened.

“See, that’s where you’re wrong,” the man said, leaning closer. “You think you can just disappear? Change your name, grow a beard, drift from town to town like some kinda tumbleweed? The man you killed, he was Mr. Kessler’s brother. And Mr. Kessler, he’s a patient man. But his patience has run out.”

The name hit Elias like a physical blow. Not his name, but a name from a life he’d buried in the desert sand a decade ago. A mission gone wrong. A face he saw in his nightmares. He’d been a weapon then, and the man he’d killed had been a target. But that was another life, another man. This was a mistake. A fatal one.

“I told you,” Elias said, his voice barely a whisper, “you have the wrong man.”

“We’ll see about that,” the leader said. He reached out, a meaty hand aiming for Elias’s shoulder. “We’re gonna take a little ride. Mr. Kessler wants to have a word.”

Time seemed to stretch, to slow to a crawl. Elias saw the hand coming, saw the expectant smirk on the man’s face, saw the shadow of the other two men closing in. The ex-soldier in him, dormant for so long, awakened with a cold, furious clarity. It wasn’t about fighting. It was about survival. It was about the geometry of the space, the leverage of the stool, the weight of the ceramic mug.

In one fluid motion, faster than a man his size should have been able to move, Elias pivoted. He didn’t go for the leader. He drove his elbow, hard and sharp, into the throat of the man on his right. The man gasped, a choked, wet sound, and stumbled back, clutching his neck. In the same instant, Elias swept the heavy ceramic mug off the counter and smashed it into the leader’s face. Coffee and blood erupted in a dark spray. The man roared, more in shock than pain, and reeled backward, his hand flying to his split brow.

The third man was already moving, pulling a knife from his belt. The blade glinted in the fluorescent light. Elias didn’t hesitate. He grabbed the leader’s stool and hurled it. It wasn’t a weapon; it was a distraction. The man with the knife flinched, and in that split second, Elias was on him. He caught the man’s wrist, twisting it with a sickening crunch. The knife clattered to the linoleum floor. A swift, brutal knee to the gut doubled the man over, and a sharp chop to the back of the neck sent him sprawling.

Silence. The only sounds were the hiss of the grill and the ragged breathing of the three men on the floor. Elias stood over them, his chest heaving, his eyes cold and distant. The ghost was gone. The soldier was back.

He reached into his pocket, pulled out a crumpled twenty-dollar bill, and dropped it on the counter. He looked at Dot, who was staring at him, her face pale, her eyes wide with a mixture of terror and awe.

“For the coffee,” he said, his voice rough. “And the mess.”

He didn’t wait for a reply. He walked out into the rain, the bell jingling a final, mournful note behind him. The cold water plastered his hair to his skull and washed the blood from his knuckles. He didn’t look back. He just kept walking, a drifter once more, but now a hunted one. The past had found him, and it wasn’t going to let go.

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
The trouble with collecting Madame Alexander dolls, Cora had long ago decided, was that everyone assumed you wanted to talk about them. She had come to the Tri-County Fairgrounds for one reason and one reason only: the 1962 Cissette in the blue taffeta, the one with the faint factory smudge on her left cheek that the seller from Ithaca had described, somewhat optimistically, as "patina." Cora had been thinking about that smudge for eleven days.

The antiques show occupied the 4-H barn, which smelled of hay and old varnish and the occasional hot dog. Cora moved down the aisles with the practiced economy of a woman who had been doing this since before most of these dealers were born. She nodded at the woman with the flow blue china. She stepped around a man arguing about the price of a butter churn. She did not stop for the carnival glass, though it was lovely, because you stop for one thing and the next thing you know it's three o'clock and the Cissette is gone.

She found the booth at the far end, past the quilt display. The seller was a round woman in a sweatshirt that said GRANDMA'S ATTIC in puffy paint, and she had the Cissette set up on a little folding table under a lamp, which was wrong, of course—direct light on the celluloid—but Cora was too relieved to see her to make a fuss. The smudge was there. The taffeta was original. The shoes, miracle of miracles, matched.

"Two hundred," the woman said, before Cora had even picked her up.

"I'll give you one-fifty."

"One seventy-five and I throw in the stand."

They settled at one sixty, and Cora was counting out bills when she heard the shouting.

It came from the next aisle over, near the tool dealers. A man's voice, high and strained, saying something about a debt, about being cheated, about how he'd been waiting three months. Cora looked up. Grandma's Attic looked up. Half the barn looked up, and then half the barn looked away again, because fairground arguments were not, as a rule, interesting, and there was a Limoges tea set two booths down that wasn't going to price itself.

Cora tucked the Cissette into her tote, wrapped in the towel she'd brought for exactly this purpose, and went to find the ladies' room. That was the thing nobody told you about getting older—you planned your whole day around the location of the nearest restroom.

The ladies' room was behind the poultry building, a cinderblock affair with a flickering fluorescent light and a hand dryer that sounded like a leaf blower. Cora was washing her hands when she noticed the door to the supply closet wasn't quite shut. And there was a shoe in the gap. A brown loafer, size eleven or thereabouts, attached to a sock, attached to a leg.

She stood very still for a moment. The hand dryer rattled to a stop. In the silence she could hear the distant bray of the loudspeaker—"Attention fairgoers, the pie judging will begin in fifteen minutes"—and nothing else at all.

Cora pushed the door open with one finger.

The man from the argument was on the floor between a mop bucket and a case of paper towels, and he was not going to be collecting any debts. There was a tack hammer by his head, the kind with the red handle, the kind you could buy at any hardware store in the county. His eyes were open and his mouth was open and Cora thought, absurdly, of the Cissette in her bag, of the smudge on her cheek, of how she'd waited eleven days for this and now here she was, and now she'd have to talk to a sheriff.

She backed out of the closet and let the door swing shut. Then she opened it again, because you weren't supposed to leave a thing like that, and stood there in the flickering light, and waited for someone else to come in.

It took four minutes. A teenager with a nose ring and a funnel cake. Cora watched her take it in—the shoe, the door, Cora's face—and watched her decide, in real time, that this was going to be the most interesting thing that happened to her all summer.

"Don't touch anything," Cora said. "And go find a deputy."

The girl went.

title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
“He’s what?” Jax’s voice cut through the humming quiet of the hydroponics bay like a dull knife. He was a big man, built like a cargo loader, and he had a habit of speaking with his whole body. Right now, his body was screaming disbelief.

Maya didn’t look up from the tomato vines she was pruning. Her movements were precise, almost surgical. “I said, the Captain is lying. Our destination isn’t Proxima Centauri b.” She snipped a dead leaf. “It never was.”

“That’s insane,” Jax boomed, taking a step forward, his heavy boots thudding on the metal grating. “We’ve been on this ship for thirty years. Thirty years of recycled air and algae burgers. My parents are in the ground because of this trip. You’re telling me it’s all been for nothing?”

“Not for nothing,” Maya said, finally turning. Her face was calm, but her eyes were sharp, analytical. She was the ship’s systems analyst, the one who saw the patterns in the data no one else bothered to look at. “Just not for Proxima.”

From the corner, a quiet voice spoke. “How do you know?” Leo, the ship’s young, nervous medic, was clutching a datapad to his chest like a shield. He looked from Maya to Jax, his eyes wide. “I mean… it’s the Captain. He’s… he’s the Captain.”

“And I’m the one who maintains the navigation logs,” Maya replied, her tone flat. “I found a ghost in the machine. A subroutine buried deep in the stellar cartography files.
