It’s been running for decades, subtly altering the long-range sensor data we’ve been getting. The real readings are… different.”

Jax ran a hand over his shaved head. “Different how? Are we lost? Are we flying into a black hole?”

“No,” Maya said, pulling up a holographic star chart from her datapad. It shimmered in the air between them. “We’re not lost. We’re just… not going where we thought.” She pointed to a small, unremarkable speck of light on the chart. “This is our actual trajectory. It’s a star system called Tau Ceti. Specifically, a moon orbiting the fourth planet.”

Leo squinted at the chart. “Tau Ceti? But… the initial probes said it was a dead system. No atmosphere, no water. That’s why they chose Proxima. It had a candidate planet.”

“Exactly,” Maya nodded. “The public story was that Tau Ceti was a bust. But the Captain’s personal files, the ones he thinks are encrypted… they tell a different story. The probes found something. Something they didn’t want to share.”

The door to the hydroponics bay hissed open, and Captain Aris stepped in. He was a slender man with a permanent furrow in his brow and a voice that was always calm, always reasonable. It was the voice he used now. “I think that’s enough, Maya.”

Jax spun around, his fists clenched. “Captain! Is it true? Are we not going to Proxima?”

Aris didn’t flinch. He looked at Jax, then at Leo’s terrified face, and finally settled his gaze on Maya. “The truth is complicated.”

“Try us,” Jax growled.

Aris sighed, a deep, weary sound. “The probes did find something at Tau Ceti. A signal. A complex, artificial signal emanating from that moon. The government, the people who funded this ship… they didn’t want a First Contact scenario. They wanted a colony. A nice, safe, predictable new home. So they buried the data and pointed us at a star we could reach and that had a planet we could theoretically terraform.”

“You knew?” Leo whispered, his voice cracking. “This whole time… you knew?”

“I was ordered to,” Aris said, his calm finally breaking, a flicker of pain in his eyes. “My job was to get you all to a new world. Safe. That was the mission. The signal was a risk. A risk of war, of disease, of… the unknown. I was told to protect the mission.”

“You lied to us,” Jax said, his voice low and dangerous. “You lied to my parents. You let them die thinking they were going to paradise.”

“I gave them purpose,” Aris shot back, his voice rising for the first time. “I gave them a goal. Hope. What would you have had me do? Tell them we were flying into the unknown, chasing a ghost signal from a dead moon? Half the ship would have mutinied.”

“Maybe they should have!” Jax roared.

“And then what?” Aris demanded. “Drift forever? We have one chance at this. One shot to survive as a species.”

Maya stepped between them, her presence a cold, logical buffer. “The signal, Captain. What did it say?”

Aris looked at her, the fight draining out of him. He looked old, suddenly. Tired. “It wasn’t a message. It was a beacon. A beacon that’s been broadcasting for thousands of years.” He paused, and the hum of the ship seemed to fill the silence. “It was a warning.”

Leo took a shaky breath. “A warning about what?”

The Captain met Maya’s steady gaze, and for the first time, she saw genuine fear in his eyes. “It was a warning to stay away.”

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The sound started just after midnight, a slow, deliberate thud against the corrugated metal of the loading dock door. Not a scrape. Not the wind. A rhythm. *Thud. Pause. Thud.*

Maya froze, a can of peaches halfway to the shelf. Across the aisle, crouched behind a toppled display of cereal, Dale held up a hand. His face, greasy with three days of sweat and fear, was a mask of strained attention. The others—the Hendersons huddled with their teenage son, and old Mr. Castille—all turned toward the sound, their eyes wide and reflecting the dim glow of the battery-powered lantern.

“Is it them?” whispered Mrs. Henderson, her voice cracking. “Did they get through the back?”

Dale shook his head slowly. He pointed two fingers at his own eyes, then at the dark, cavernous back of the store where the loading dock was. He was the closest thing they had to a leader, a former security guard who’d gotten them this far. He motioned for Maya to stay put and began a low, careful crawl toward the noise.

*Thud. Pause. Thud.*

It was too steady. Too patient. The infected, the ones they’d seen, were frenzied, all gnashing teeth and scrabbling claws. They didn’t knock.

Maya’s heart hammered against her ribs. She remembered the sound of the shovel. The wet, heavy *chuff* of earth. The way they’d all stood in the rain, not speaking, as they’d covered the bodies in the shallow grave behind the garden center. They’d buried four of them that day. Including Leo.

Leo, who had taught her how to fix a broken pallet jack. Leo, who had a stupid joke for every situation. Leo, who had been bitten on the ankle while they were clearing the pharmacy and had begged them to end it before he turned.

The knocking stopped. A new sound replaced it, a soft, dragging noise, like a sack of potatoes being pulled across concrete. Then, a voice, muffled by the steel door but unmistakable.

“Maya? Dale? You guys in there?”

The can of peaches slipped from Maya’s fingers, clattering to the floor and rolling into the darkness. The sound was deafening in the silence.

Dale had frozen mid-crawl. He looked back at her, his eyes asking a question she couldn’t answer.

“It’s Leo,” she breathed, the name a ghost on her lips.

“No,” Dale mouthed, shaking his head violently. “No, it’s not.”

“Guys, come on,” the voice came again, a little louder, a little more insistent. It had Leo’s easy, slightly raspy tone. “It’s cold out here. I think… I think I got turned around. Open up.”

Mr. Castille, who had been silent for days, suddenly stood up, his eyes wild. “We have to let him in!” he croaked. “Dear God, he’s alive!”

“Shut up!” Dale hissed, scrambling back to them. “That’s not Leo. We put a bullet in Leo’s head and buried him. You were there, Castille. You saw.”

“But it sounds just like him!” the old man pleaded.

“That’s what they do,” Maya said, her voice trembling but firm. She’d seen it before, on a supply run. A thing that had worn the face of a woman’s husband, mimicking his voice to lure her from a barricaded house. “They mimic. They remember.”

*Thud. THUD. THUD.*

The knocking was harder now, more demanding. The metal door groaned under the impact.

“Maya!” Leo’s voice was no longer friendly. It was sharp, edged with a cold frustration. “I know you’re in there. I can smell you. Open the damn door!”

The Hendersons’ son started to cry, a quiet, hopeless whimper. Mrs. Henderson clamped a hand over his mouth, her own face streaked with tears.

“We can’t just ignore him,” Mr. Castille argued, wringing his hands. “What if it is him? What if he dug himself out?”

“Then he’d be a rotting corpse with a hole in his skull,” Dale snarled, grabbing the old man by the collar. “Now get back and shut your mouth before you get us all killed.”

He shoved Castille back toward the others and turned to Maya. His eyes were hard. “We don’t answer. We don’t make a sound. It’ll get bored and go away.”

But they knew better. The knocking continued, a relentless, patient drumbeat against their sanctuary. And then, the voice came one last time, clear and chillingly calm, as if it were standing right on the other side of the door, its lips pressed to the metal.

“I’ll just wait,” it said. “I’m very good at waiting.”

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
The first thing I noticed was the cold. It wasn’t the gentle, bracing chill of a winter morning, but a deep, bone-seeking freeze that clawed its way through the silk of my blouse and settled in my marrow. The second thing I noticed was the smell. A strange, metallic tang, like a mouthful of pennies, that cut through the sterile, frost-bitten air.

And the third thing, the thing my brain refused to process for a full, horrifying ten seconds, was the body.

Leo was propped up against a shelf of frozen dinner rolls, his tuxedo jacket a stark slash of black against the silver shelving. A bag of peas had tumbled from a higher shelf and rested near his hip, a grotesque, emerald-green garnish. His face was a pale, waxy blue, and a thin ribbon of crimson had frozen solid on his temple, a macabre icicle against his skin.

My hand flew to my mouth, but no sound came out. Just a strangled, airless gasp. I stumbled back, my heel catching on the rubber mat, and my hand shot out to brace myself against the doorframe. The metal was so cold it felt like a burn.

*Okay, Clara. Think. Breathe. You’ve handled a bridezilla who wanted live peacocks. You’ve survived a groomsman who lost the rings down a storm drain. You can handle this.*

But my legs weren't listening. They felt like they were filled with wet sand. I could feel my heart hammering against my ribs, a frantic, trapped bird. This wasn't a seating chart crisis. This was… this was a dead best man.

Leo. Charming, roguish Leo, who’d spent the entire rehearsal dinner flirting with the maid of honor and telling terrible jokes that somehow still made everyone laugh. He was supposed to be giving a speech tomorrow. A speech he’d been agonizing over for weeks. He’d shown me three different drafts, all of them too long and too full of inside jokes no one else would understand. I’d told him to just speak from the heart.

Now his heart had stopped.

I forced myself to look again, my gaze sweeping over the scene. The freezer was a walk-in, the kind a high-end hotel uses for bulk storage. It was meticulously organized, shelves labeled and stocked. Nothing seemed out of place. Except for the dead body. A crate of lemons was overturned near his feet, a few of the bright yellow spheres scattered across the floor like fallen stars. Had he been reaching for them? Why would he be in here at all?

The door. The heavy, industrial door with its thick rubber seal. It wasn't locked from the outside. I’d just pulled the handle and it had swung open. But on the inside… my eyes found the release latch. It was a simple, glow-in-the-dark lever. A safety feature. It was firmly in the ‘open’ position. So he hadn’t been trapped. He’d come in here, and someone had followed him. Or he’d been brought here.

“Clara? Are you down here?”

The voice, cheerful and laced with a hint of impatience, sliced through the silence. It was Marcus, the hotel’s banquet manager. My heart leaped into my throat. I couldn't let him see this. Not yet.

I stepped back and pulled the heavy door shut, the seal closing with a soft, final *whoosh*. I leaned against it, my back to the cold metal, trying to compose myself. My breath came out in little white puffs.

Marcus rounded the corner, his perfectly coiffed hair and gleaming name tag a stark contrast to the chaos erupting in my mind. “There you are. The bride’s mother is asking for more champagne, and she’s got that look in her eye. You know the one. The ‘my daughter’s wedding will be a disaster and it’s all your fault’ look.”

I stared at him. Champagne. He was talking about champagne. My mind was a frantic scramble of images—Leo’s blue lips, the frozen blood, the bag of peas. “Marcus,” I said, my voice a thin, reedy whisper. I cleared my throat, trying to inject some authority into it. “Marcus, I need you to do something for me.”

He raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow. “Of course. More champagne?”

“No. I need you to get the hotel manager. And… and security. And don’t let anyone come down this hallway. Not a single soul.”

His smile faltered. He finally registered the look on my face, the way I was plastered against the freezer door like I was holding back the hounds of hell. “Clara? What’s wrong? You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”

I swallowed hard, the metallic taste of fear still thick in my throat. *A ghost would be easier,* I thought. *A ghost doesn’t need a coroner and a police report and a very, very good explanation.*

“Worse,” I said, my voice finally steady. “I think I’ve just seen the end of my career.”

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
The diary was bound in soft blue leather, the kind of thing you’d pick up at a stationery shop on a whim, and it smelled faintly of the lavender sachets Ellen kept in her lingerie drawer. Mark turned it over in his hands. He had found it wedged between the mattress and the bed frame while changing the sheets—sheets that still carried the ghost of antiseptic from the hospital, though Ellen had been home for three weeks now. Three weeks of the ventilator’s hiss replaced by the dry rattle of the humidifier, of nurses’ brisk efficiency replaced by the hospice aide who came twice a day and spoke too loudly, as if volume could penetrate the silence his wife had fallen into.

He shouldn’t read it. He knew that. A man’s wife tries to kill herself, leaves a note that says only *I’m sorry, I can’t*, and the husband is supposed to respect her privacy? The thought curdled in his chest. Privacy was for people who planned to wake up.

He sat on the edge of the bed, the diary cool against his palms, and opened to the first page. The handwriting was Ellen’s—looping, precise, the letters leaning forward as if eager to escape the line. The date was from fourteen months ago.

*October 3rd. M. asked about the life insurance again tonight. Not in a cruel way. He was passing the peas. “Did you ever get the beneficiary form notarized?” Just like that. I said I’d do it this week. He nodded and asked if I wanted more wine. I wanted to scream. I wanted to ask him why he needs to know the exact dollar amount my death would be worth. But I didn’t. I smiled and said the roast was dry.*

Mark stopped. He remembered that dinner. The roast had been dry. He’d said so. Ellen had laughed and said, “You try cooking a brisket when the oven runs twenty degrees hot.” He hadn’t thought about the insurance question at all. It was paperwork. Grown-up paperwork. He’d been proud of them for handling it.

He turned the page.

*November 17th. Found a hair in the bathroom sink this morning. Blonde. I’m a brunette. M. says it’s from the cleaning lady, but Rosa has black hair and comes on Thursdays. Today is Monday. I put the hair in a Ziploc bag and hid it in my sock drawer. I don’t know why. I don’t know what I think I’m collecting. Evidence? For whom?*

Mark’s jaw tightened. The cleaning lady. That was reasonable. Rosa’s daughter sometimes helped her, didn’t she? A blonde daughter, maybe. He tried to picture Rosa’s daughter. He couldn’t. He turned another page, faster now.

*December 24th. Christmas Eve. M. fell asleep on the couch at nine. I sat in the kitchen and ate three cookies and listened to the furnace kick on and off. I thought: this is what dying must feel like. Everything warm and humming and completely indifferent. I wrote him a letter. I didn’t give it to him. I put it in the blue diary instead. Maybe someday he’ll find it and understand that I wasn’t angry. I was just so tired of being the only one who noticed the silence.*

The hospice aide’s key scraped in the lock downstairs. Mark froze, then shoved the diary under his pillow. He heard her call out, “Mr. Hendricks? I’m here for Ellen’s bath.” He stood, smoothed the bedspread, and walked to the door.

“She’s resting,” he said. “Can you come back in an hour?”

The aide—Carla, her name was Carla—frowned. “She’s supposed to get the sponge bath every day, Mr. Hendricks. Doctor’s orders.”

“An hour,” Mark repeated. His voice came out harder than he intended. Carla’s eyebrows lifted. She was young, maybe twenty-five, with a nose ring and a tattoo of a hummingbird on her wrist. Ellen had liked her. Ellen had said, *She doesn’t treat me like a piece of furniture.*

“Everything okay?” Carla asked.

“Fine. Just—give us an hour.”

He closed the door and went back to the bed. The diary was still warm from his body. He opened it to a page near the end, his hands trembling now.

*February 9th. I called the bank today. The account I opened in my maiden name has $4,200 in it. I’ve been saving for a year. Not enough to leave. Enough to disappear for a while. I looked up bus schedules to Portland. I don’t know anyone in Portland. That’s the point. M. came home at six. He asked what was for dinner. I said, “I don’t know, what are you making?” He laughed. He actually laughed. As if I’d made a joke. As if I hadn’t just asked him to see me.*

Mark closed the diary. His hands were shaking so badly he had to press them flat against his thighs. From the bed, Ellen breathed on, slow and even, her face slack and pale against the pillow. The humidifier burbled. Somewhere outside, a dog barked twice and then stopped.

He looked at his wife—really looked, the way he hadn’t in years—and wondered who she’d been writing to. Because those words weren’t for him. Those words were for someone else entirely, someone she’d hoped would find them. And Mark understood, with a cold, sinking certainty, that he was not that person.

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The rain had stopped, but the city still smelled of it—wet stone, diesel, the faint green rot of the canals. Commissario Brunetti—no, let’s call him Lo Specchio, the Mirror, because that’s what the Questura called him, and he’d stopped fighting it—stood in the doorway of the widow’s apartment on the second floor of a building near Santa Maria Formosa. The door was open before he knocked. She’d been waiting.

“Commissario.” She stepped back, one hand on the doorframe. Fifty-odd, maybe sixty. A cardigan the color of oatmeal, buttons mismatched. No jewelry except a thin gold band on her right hand, not her left. “You’ll want coffee. I made it already. It’s the moka, not the machine. The machine broke in March.”

He followed her through a narrow hallway. A mirror—ironic—hung crooked, and he straightened it without thinking. The living room had tall windows, shutters open, and the light was that flat, exhausted gray that Venice gets in November. A man’s overcoat still hung on a hook by the door. Brown wool. Too big for her.

“Signora Vianello,” he said. “My condolences.”

She turned from the stove. “Thank you.” She said it the way you thank a cashier. Then, quieter: “Sit. Please. The cups are here.”

He sat. The table was Formica, a pattern of little gold flecks. She set down two cups, a sugar bowl with a chip in the lid, and a plate of store-bought biscuits—the kind in the plastic tray, the kind nobody actually likes. He noticed she hadn’t touched the biscuits herself. She drank her coffee black, no sugar, and watched him over the rim.

“You found him,” she said. Not a question.

“A fisherman did. Near the Canale di San Pietro. This morning, around six.”

“He hated that canal.” She set her cup down. “He said it smelled like a dead dog. He was right.” A pause. “Was it quick?”

Lo Specchio had seen the body. The back of the skull, the way the water had done its work. “We think so,” he said. It was a lie, but a small one, the kind you give widows.

She nodded. Then she did something that made him put down his own cup. She smiled. Not a big smile—a private one, the kind you might give a memory. It lasted a second and a half, maybe two, and then it was gone, but he’d seen it.

“Signora,” he said, “when did you last see your husband?”

“Tuesday. He left after lunch. Said he had a meeting with a man about a boat.” She folded her hands on the table. “He was always meeting men about boats. He didn’t own a boat. He didn’t even like boats. But he liked the men who owned them. They lent him money.”

“And you?”

“I lent him nothing. I have a pension from the post office. It’s small. He couldn’t get his hands on it.” She said this without bitterness. It was a fact, like the rain.

Lo Specchio turned his cup a quarter turn. “You don’t seem surprised.”

“I’m not.”

“Why?”

She looked past him, at the window, at the gray light on the water. “Because he was a man who made lists of enemies and then forgot to cross them off. He owed everyone. The butcher. The man at the tabacchi. A woman in Mestre whose name he said in his sleep.” She paused. “I stopped sleeping in the same room three years ago. The couch is not comfortable, but it’s honest.”

He waited. The radiator ticked.

“You want to know if I killed him,” she said. “I didn’t. I’m not brave enough. But I’ll tell you what I am.” She leaned forward, and her voice dropped, not to a whisper but to something lower, more solid. “I’m relieved. Is that a crime? To be relieved?”

Lo Specchio thought about the overcoat on the hook. The mismatched buttons. The way she’d made coffee for two before he’d even knocked. “No,” he said. “It’s not a crime.”

She stood up and took his cup to the sink. “Then we’re done,” she said. “Unless you want a biscuit. They’re stale. I bought them for the funeral. I don’t know why. Nobody eats at funerals.”

He took one. It was stale. He ate it anyway, because she was watching, and because the rain had started again, and because somewhere out there a man had died in a canal that smelled like a dead dog, and the widow was already washing the cups.

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The summons came at midnight, sealed with the royal crest and delivered by a boy too young to know fear. Lyra read it twice, then tossed it into the fire.

“They’re desperate,” she told the flames, which flickered in a way that suggested agreement. “The great Prince Aldric, poisoned by his own ambition. How tragic.”

She had spent three years in exile, scraping a living from hedge-witchery and the occasional love potion for farmers’ daughters. Her robes were patched. Her staff was a walking stick she’d stolen from a scarecrow. And she had never been happier.

The second summons came at dawn, delivered by a woman in captain’s armor who did not wait for an invitation.

“Lady Lyra,” the captain said, stepping over the threshold without wiping her boots. “The prince is dying.”

“I heard.” Lyra didn’t look up from the pot of porridge she was stirring. “Tell His Highness I wish him a swift and painless transition.”

“He asked for you.”

That made her laugh—a sharp, ugly sound. “Did he? Or did his advisors ask for me because the court physicians have run out of leeches?”

The captain’s jaw tightened. “He said your name. Twice. Before the fever took his wits.”

Lyra stopped stirring.

---

The palace smelled the same. Beeswax and betrayal.

They’d put her in the east tower, the one with the draft that whistled through the stones like a dying man’s breath. The same tower she’d been locked in for three days before her exile, while Aldric decided whether to execute her or merely ruin her.

“Cozy,” she said, dropping her bag on the cot. “You’ve kept my accommodations exactly as I remember.”

The captain—Mira, she’d learned, a woman who spoke in clipped sentences and never blinked—stood guard at the door. “You’ll see him at noon. The physicians have bled him twice. He has perhaps a week.”

“A week.” Lyra unpacked her herbs, her crystals, her one good knife. “And what, precisely, am I meant to do in a week that your royal physicians cannot?”

“You’re the only one who’s ever cured the blackroot poison.”

Lyra paused. “I cured a goat. Once. Twenty years ago. And I was showing off for a boy I liked.”

“The prince remembers.”

“The prince,” Lyra said, “remembers nothing but his own reflection.”

---

Aldric looked smaller than she remembered.

The fever had hollowed him out, turned his golden skin grey and his sharp cheekbones into blades. He lay propped against a mountain of pillows, his nightshirt soaked through with sweat, his eyes closed. The royal physicians hovered like vultures in clean aprons.

“Out,” Lyra said.

They looked to the captain. Mira nodded. They filed out.

Lyra pulled a stool to the bedside and sat. For a long moment, she just looked at him—this boy who had been her student, her friend, her king, her executioner.

“I know you’re awake,” she said. “Your breathing’s wrong.”

Aldric’s eyes opened. They were the same impossible blue, but the arrogance had burned out of them. What remained was something raw and frightened.

“You came,” he rasped.

“I was summoned. There’s a difference.”

“I thought you’d refuse.”

“I did. Twice.” She pulled a vial from her pocket and uncorked it. “Open.”

He obeyed. The medicine was bitter—she’d made sure of that—and he grimaced as it went down.

“Blackroot,” she said, recapping the vial. “Someone’s been feeding it to you for months. Small doses. Enough to make you paranoid, then sick, then dead. It mimics a dozen other ailments. Your physicians never stood a chance.”

“Who?”

“I have theories.” She leaned back. “But first, you’re going to apologize.”

Aldric blinked. “What?”

“You heard me. You exiled me. You stripped my name, my title, my lands. You told the entire court I’d tried to poison you—the irony of which is not lost on me, by the way—and you did it because your advisors whispered that I was too powerful, too influential, too *dangerous*. And you believed them.”

His jaw worked. “I was young.”

“You were twenty-three. Old enough to know better.”

“You made me look weak.” The words burst out of him, fever-bright and honest. “You were always there, always correcting me, always right. The court laughed behind my back. They called me your puppet.”

Lyra stared at him. “So you cut my strings.”

“I didn’t want to be your puppet.”

“And now?”

He was silent for a long moment. Then: “Now I’m dying, and the only person who can save me is the one person I was too proud to keep.”

Lyra stood. “Apology accepted.”

“I didn’t apologize.”

“You will. Later. When you’re not dying.” She pulled a small knife from her belt and pricked her finger, letting a drop of blood fall into a bowl of water. It swirled, darkened, formed shapes. “Your poisoner is close. Someone who has access to your food, your wine, your chambers. Someone you trust.”

Aldric’s face went paler still. “Who?”

The water showed a face. Lyra’s mouth tightened.

“Your uncle,” she said. “The Duke of Ashford.”

Aldric closed his eyes. “He raised me. After my parents died. He—”

“He wanted the throne. You were in the way. And he knew that if he moved against you directly, I would have stopped him.” She smiled grimly. “So he got rid of me first.”

“Lyra—”

“Save it.” She pulled a second vial from her pocket, this one filled with a thick amber liquid. “Drink this. It’ll hurt. A lot. But it’ll flush the poison from your system.”

“And then?”

“And then we catch a duke.” She held the vial to his lips. “And you’re going to make a very public apology. In front of the entire court. About how you were wrong about me. About how you were a fool. About how I’m the best thing that ever happened to this kingdom.”

Aldric drank. His face contorted with pain. But he managed a weak, wheezing laugh.

“You’re enjoying this,” he said.

Lyra smiled—the first real smile in three years.

“Immensely,” she said.

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
The round cooked off inside the T-7’s turret. A brief, brilliant flare behind the vision blocks, then nothing but static on the comms and a column of black smoke that bent sideways in the wind.

“Scratch one,” Vasquez said. Her voice was flat, all the emotion burned out of it hours ago. She was the commander of the remaining tank, the *Harrower*, a fifty-ton block of scarred composite and bad attitude.

“They’re flanking us,” her driver, Kessler, reported. His voice was tight. “Grid four, moving fast. Light armor.”

“I see them.” Vasquez chewed her lip. The colony’s main processing plant was a half-kilometer behind them, a sprawling mess of conveyors and crushers they’d been ordered to hold. The contract was simple: keep the miners safe, keep the ore flowing. The invaders, a well-equipped corporate outfit with a hard-on for annexation, had other ideas.

“Gunner,” she said. “HEAT. Target the lead vehicle.”

“Identified,” came the reply from the turret. A pause. “On the way.”

The *Harrower* shuddered, the 120mm cannon roaring. Downrange, a wheeled APC blossomed into a ball of fire. The vehicles behind it swerved, breaking formation.

“Good hit,” Kessler said. “They’re pulling back.”

“They’re not pulling back. They’re repositioning.” Vasquez wiped sweat and grime from her forehead. The air in the turret was thick with the smell of cordite and hot metal. They’d been at this for six hours. The first wave had been easy, a probe. The second had been a real fight. This third one was a meat grinder. They’d started with four tanks. Now they were one.

The comms crackled. “*Harrower*, this is Overwatch. Be advised, multiple inbound tracks from the north. Looks like their main effort.”

“How many?” Vasquez asked.

“I count eight. Repeat, eight. Heavies.”

Kessler swore under his breath. Eight against one. Those were suicide numbers.

“Copy, Overwatch. We’ll hold.”

She switched to the internal channel. “You heard the man. We’ve got eight heavies coming from the north. We’re it. The last line before the colony.”

“So, we’re dead,” the gunner said. It wasn’t a question.

“We’re mercenaries,” Vasquez corrected. “We’re dead if we don’t get paid. And we don’t get paid if the colony falls.” She pulled up the tactical map on her display. The northern approach was a natural chokepoint, a narrow valley between two slag heaps. “Kessler, get us to grid six-alpha. We’ll use the slag heaps for cover. Make them come at us one at a time.”

“They’ll just call in artillery,” Kessler argued.

“Then we make sure we’re not there when it lands. Move.”

The *Harrower* lurched forward, its engine straining. The tank was a mess, its side skirts scarred and dented from a dozen near misses. One of the headlights was smashed. It was a brute, but it was their brute.

They reached the chokepoint just as the first enemy tank nosed into the valley. It was a sleek, predatory thing, all angles and composite armor. Vasquez didn’t recognize the model. Didn’t matter.

“Gunner, sabot. Aim for the tracks.”

“On the way.”

The *Harrower* fired. The round caught the lead tank on its left track, blowing it apart. The enemy tank slewed sideways, blocking the path for the one behind it.

“Hit! He’s crippled!”

“Shift fire. Target the second one.”

Another shot. Another hit. The valley was becoming a junkyard. But the others were learning. They were backing off, using the wrecks for cover.

“They’re getting smart,” Kessler said. “They’re going to try and flank us through the slag.”

“Let them,” Vasquez said. She was already calculating the angles. This wasn’t a battle anymore. It was a siege, and they were the castle. A very small, very angry castle with one gun.

“Overwatch to *Harrower*,” the comms chirped. “We’ve got a situation. The miners… they’re refusing to evacuate. They’ve barricaded themselves in the main shaft.”

Vasquez closed her eyes for a second. Of course they had. Brave, stupid, or both. It didn’t matter. It just made the job harder. “Tell them we’re working on it.”

She opened her eyes and stared at the tactical display. Eight red icons. One blue one. The math was simple. The outcome was not.

“Kessler,” she said, her voice low and hard. “Load the last of the AP. We’re going to make a hole.”

“And then?”

“And then we drive through it.”

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The guy in the driver’s seat—Danny, though he’d been “Danny Boy” so long the name felt like a bad joke—had a way of drumming his fingers on the steering wheel that made me want to chew glass. Tap-tap-tap-tap. A syncopated little rhythm, like a nervous heartbeat. The engine was off, but the car still held the day’s heat, a suffocating pocket of stale air and Danny’s cheap cologne. Outside, the world was a smear of rain on the windshield, the streetlights of this nothing suburb bleeding into yellow halos.

“It’s a kid, Danny,” I said, for what felt like the tenth time. My voice was a low rasp in the close quarters. “We don’t do kids.”

Tap-tap-tap-tap. “It’s not a *kid* kid. He’s twelve. That’s practically a teenager. He’s got a phone, he’s got opinions. He’s not a baby.”

“He’s a baby,” I insisted, staring at the side of his face. He had a weak chin, I decided. A weak chin and a weak plan. “A rich baby. That’s worse. That’s a headline. ‘Innocent Child of Local Surgeon Snatched from…” I trailed off, gesturing vaguely at the manicured lawns and silent, dark-windowed houses. “…from Pleasantville.”

“The surgeon part is the point, Mickey. The point is the money. You saw the house. You saw the car. He’s got more money than God and he probably doesn’t even lock his doors.” Danny finally stopped drumming and turned to look at me. His eyes were too bright, fueled by something I didn’t trust. Desperation, maybe. Or stupidity. They were often the same thing. “This is our shot. No more nickel-and-dime B&Es. No more fencing stolen TVs for a hundred bucks a pop. This is the big one.”

I sank lower in the passenger seat, the worn leather creaking in protest. The big one. In Danny’s world, “the big one” was always just around the corner, usually attached to a scheme with more holes than a fishing net. I’d been along for the ride for five years, ever since we were both dumb and nineteen, and the ride had been mostly a series of potholes. But this… this was a different road entirely.

My gut was screaming at me. It had been screaming since Danny had first laid out the plan on a napkin in a diner two days ago, his finger tracing the layout of the surgeon’s house, the kid’s school schedule, the blind spot in the security system. It was a good plan, on paper. Too good. The kind of plan that makes you feel smart right up until the moment the handcuffs click shut.

“What about the mother?” I asked, playing my last card. “You said she’s always home. What are we supposed to do with her? Tie her up? Look her in the eye while her kid is screaming for her? You up for that, Danny? You up for being *that* guy?”

He flinched, just a little. A tiny crack in the facade. I saw it. He was picturing it, same as me. The terror in a woman’s eyes. The high, thin wail of a scared child. It was a sound that could burrow into your skull and live there forever. I knew it. He didn’t. Not yet.

“We won’t have to look her in the eye,” he said, his voice a little too loud, a little too defensive. “We wear masks. We’re in and out in ten minutes. We get the kid, we make the call, we get the cash. Simple. He’ll be home by dinner. No one gets hurt.”

“No one gets hurt,” I repeated, the words tasting like ash. “You keep saying that like it’s a magic spell. It’s not. It’s a lie we tell ourselves so we can sleep at night. But you won’t sleep, Danny. Not after this. Not ever. You’ll see that kid’s face every time you close your eyes.”

He was quiet for a long moment. The rain intensified, drumming a frantic rhythm on the roof of the car. It was a sound that matched the one in my chest. I could feel the weight of the decision pressing down on us, thick and heavy as the humid air. This was the fork in the road. The point of no return. We could start the engine, drive away, and pretend this conversation never happened. Go back to boosting car stereos and petty burglary. It was a shitty life, but it was a life. We could still come out the other side of it.

Or we could get out of this car and walk into that house.

Danny took a deep, shaky breath. He didn’t look at me. He just stared straight ahead through the rain-slicked glass, his knuckles white on the wheel.

“It’s a quarter of a million dollars, Mickey,” he whispered, the numbers hanging in the air between us like a promise and a threat. “We just have to be brave enough to take it.”

He was wrong. It wasn’t about being brave. It was about being dead inside. And I was beginning to realize that Danny Boy was already halfway there.

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The storm had been threatening all afternoon, a bruise-colored wall of cloud swallowing the mountains one ridge at a time. By the time the first flakes fell, fat and deliberate, Dr. Elena Marsh was already regretting every choice that had led her to this windswept corner of the valley.

She’d come for a colicking mare. A simple call, two hours at most. But the mare’s owner—Cole Barrett, a man whose stubbornness was apparently legendary even by rancher standards—had insisted on helping her restrain the horse, and then on making her coffee “for the road,” and then the road had disappeared under a white fury that turned the world into a featureless blur.

Now the ranch house windows rattled in their frames, and the wind moaned down the chimney like something wounded.

“You’re not going anywhere in that.” Cole stood at the kitchen window, one hand braced against the frame, his silhouette broad and unyielding against the swirling white. He hadn’t shaved in days; the dark stubble along his jaw caught the lamplight. “The pass’ll be drifted shut by now.”

Elena wrapped her hands around the mug he’d given her—chipped enamel, the handle worn smooth—and tried to ignore the way her pulse had quickened at his nearness. “I have a clinic to open tomorrow. Animals don’t stop getting sick because of snow.”

“They don’t. But you will, if you try that road tonight.” He turned, and his eyes—gray as the storm outside, she noticed, gray and steady—held hers. “I’ve lived here forty-two years. I know what a killing storm looks like. This is one.”

She wanted to argue. She was good at arguing; grief had made her sharp, had honed her edges until everything felt like a fight. But the truth was, her hands were still shaking from the cold, and the mare’s colic had taken more out of her than she’d admitted. And Cole Barrett, for all his gruffness, had a fire going and a pot of stew simmering and a spare bedroom he’d offered without a flicker of expectation.

“Fine,” she said, and the word came out softer than she intended. “But I’m not sleeping in your bed.”

A ghost of a smile crossed his face. “Didn’t ask you to.”

---

The power went out at eight. Cole lit lanterns and set them on the table between them, and they ate stew in a silence that was almost comfortable. The wind screamed outside, and snow piled against the door in a drift that would be waist-high by morning.

“You were good with her,” Cole said finally, not looking up from his bowl. “The mare. She trusts you.”

“She was scared. Most animals are, when they’re hurting. They just need someone to be calm with them.”

He nodded slowly. “People too.”

Elena set down her spoon. “Is that what you need, Mr. Barrett? Someone to be calm with you?”

His gaze lifted, and something flickered there—surprise, maybe, or the raw edge of loneliness he’d been carrying so long he’d forgotten how to put it down. “I don’t need anyone.”

“No,” she said quietly. “I didn’t either. After my husband died, I thought—I thought if I just kept moving, kept working, I wouldn’t have to feel it.” She hadn’t meant to say that. The words had slipped out, loosened by the storm and the lantern light and the strange intimacy of being snowed in with a stranger. “It doesn’t work, by the way.”

Cole was silent for a long moment. Then he reached across the table and covered her hand with his. His palm was rough, calloused, warm. “I know,” he said, and his voice was low, scraped raw. “I know it doesn’t.”

The lantern flickered. Outside, the storm raged on, but inside, the world had narrowed to the space between their hands, to the slow exhale of two people who had been alone too long.

“You’re still shaking,” he said.

“I’m cold.”

“Come here.”

She should have said no. She should have pulled her hand away and gone to the spare room and closed the door and waited for morning. But instead she stood, and he stood, and he pulled her against his chest—not gentle, not tentative, but sure, like he’d been waiting for permission. She pressed her face into the wool of his shirt and breathed him in: woodsmoke, coffee, snow.

“This doesn’t mean anything,” she murmured against his collar.

His hand came up to cradle the back of her head. “No,” he agreed, his voice rumbling through her. “Nothing at all.”

But they both knew he was lying.

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The rain had stopped, but the city still dripped. Commissario Brunetti—no, not Brunetti, that was someone else’s city—Commissario Vianello stood in the doorway of the widow’s apartment and tried not to drip on her floor. He was a large man, and wet, and he took up more space than he wanted to.

She had the door open before he knocked twice. Elena Moro, forty-one, in a black dress that looked like it had come off a rack that morning, tags maybe still on it. Her hair was done. Not funeral-parlor done, but done. He had seen a lot of widows in his time and most of them looked like they’d been hit by a truck. She looked like she’d slept eight hours.

“Commissario,” she said. “Come in. I’ve made coffee.”

The apartment was on the second floor of a building near Santa Maria Formosa, the kind with a courtyard that smelled of cat and old stone. Inside it was cool and dim and spotless. A man’s coat still hung on the rack by the door—a good coat, navy wool, too big for her. She hadn’t moved it. That was something. Or it was nothing.

He sat where she pointed, a chair with a view of the canal. A water bus went by and the whole room rocked with its wake, the glasses in the cabinet ticking against each other.

“You found him,” she said. Not a question.

“Yes. This morning. I’m sorry.”

She poured the coffee. Her hand was steady. He watched it and thought about the way steady hands could be a kind of lie, or a kind of truth, and you couldn’t tell which until later.

“He was in the water,” Vianello said. “Near the Riva. A fisherman found him.”

“He couldn’t swim,” she said. “Did you know that? Forty-six years old, born on this island, and he couldn’t swim. He was afraid of it. Wouldn’t even wade.”

Vianello wrote that down. He wrote slowly, because he had learned that people will fill a silence if you let them, and what they fill it with is usually worth more than the question.

She didn’t fill it.

“When did you last see him?” he asked.

“Tuesday morning. He left for work. He’s—he was—in shipping. Offices near the station. He didn’t come home Tuesday night. I assumed—” She stopped. Started again. “I assumed he was with someone. He had someone. A woman, I mean. I’ve known for about a year.”

She said it the way you’d say the roof needs fixing. Vianello kept his pen moving.

“You weren’t worried.”

“I was angry. There’s a difference.” She looked at the window, at the grey water. “Tuesday night I slept fine. Wednesday I slept fine. Last night I slept fine. And then this morning you knock on my door and I feel—” She searched for it. “I feel like I can breathe. Is that terrible? Don’t answer that.”

He didn’t.

“Where were you Tuesday night?”

“Here. Alone. The neighbor across the courtyard, the old woman with the parrot, she’ll tell you my light was on until eleven. I was reading. I read a lot now. I’ve been reading a lot for a year.”

Vianello drank his coffee. It was good, which somehow made it worse. He thought about the coat by the door, the navy wool, and how she hadn’t moved it, and how a woman who was grieving might leave a coat there for months, and a woman who was relieved might leave it there too, for different reasons, and how the coat didn’t know anything either way.

“The woman,” he said. “Do you know her name?”

“No. He was careful. Careful in a way that made it obvious.” She set her cup down. “You think I did it.”

“I didn’t say that.”

“You didn’t have to. You’re sitting there like a man doing arithmetic.” She almost smiled. “I didn’t. But I’ll tell you what I did do. In March I opened a separate account and started moving money into it. Small amounts. I was planning to leave him. That’s my crime, Commissario. I was planning to leave him and I was taking my time about it, and now he’s dead and I don’t have to.”

The water bus went by again. The glasses ticked.

Vianello closed his notebook. He had a body in the morgue with water in the lungs and a bump on the back of the head that might have been the bridge footing and might have been something else, and he had a widow who was either the best liar he’d met in twenty years or a woman who had simply run out of grief before her husband ran out of life.

“I’ll need the account number,” he said.

“I’ll get it.”

She stood. The black dress hung on her a little wrong, as if she’d bought it for a funeral that hadn’t happened yet.

“Commissario,” she said, at the door. “The coat. Should I—?”

“Leave it,” he said. “For now.”

He walked down the stairs into the wet courtyard. The cat was there. The parrot was screaming something from across the way, some phrase it had learned from the old woman, or from someone else. Vianello stood in the drizzle and listened to it and couldn’t make out the words.

title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
The rain hadn’t stopped for three days, and the station house smelled of wet wool and burnt coffee. Officer Reyes was finishing his report when the old woman appeared at the counter, water dripping from the hem of her coat, a plastic rain bonnet tied under her chin like a babushka.

“I want to report a death,” she said.

Reyes looked up. “Ma’am?”

“My husband. Vincent. He died eleven years ago tonight.” She said it the way someone might announce a bus delay. “I’ve been meaning to tell someone.”

Reyes set down his pen. “I’m not sure I follow.”

“There’s a bench by the window,” she said. “I’ll sit. You’ll listen. Then you can decide if it’s a crime.”

He brought her a cup of the burnt coffee. She wrapped her hands around it but didn’t drink.

“Vincent was a locksmith,” she began. “Forty years. He could open anything. Doors, safes, padlocks, hearts—he used to say that last one, and I’d tell him to save it for the customers.”

“Mrs.—”

“Ruth. Just Ruth.”

“Ruth. Why are you telling me this now?”

She looked at him over the rim of the cup. “Because I lied to the police then. And I’m eighty-three. I don’t want to lie anymore.”

Reyes pulled a chair around and sat. “Okay.”

“That night—November twelfth, 2013—Vincent came home late. He’d been at the shop. He had a cut on his hand, here.” She traced her own palm. “Said he’d nicked himself on a lock. But he was pale. And he wouldn’t look at me.”

“Was he ill?”

“He was scared.” She said the word plainly, like a stone set on a table. “Vincent wasn’t a scared man. He’d walked into burning buildings to open doors for people trapped inside. But that night his hands shook at supper.”

“Did he tell you why?”

“He said, ‘Ruth, I opened the wrong door tonight.’ I asked what he meant. He said a man had come to the shop—a young man, polite, paid cash. Wanted a safe opened. Vincent said the man’s hands were soft. Too soft. And he had a photograph in his coat pocket, a woman, and he kept touching it.”

Reyes waited.

“Vincent opened the safe. Inside was a gun. And money. And a letter with a name on it—the name of a man who lived on our street. Our street, officer. Three doors down.”

“Did he go to the police?”

“He was going to. In the morning. He said, ‘Ruth, I’ll call them first thing.’ But he didn’t sleep. He sat in the kitchen with the light off, and I could hear him breathing.” She paused. “At two in the morning, someone knocked.”

Reyes leaned forward.

“Three knocks. Soft. Vincent stood up. I said, ‘Don’t answer it.’ He said, ‘Ruth, if I don’t answer it, they’ll come through the window.’ He was right. So he opened the door.”

“Who was there?”

“The young man. And another one behind him. The young man said, ‘You opened my safe.’ Vincent said, ‘I did. And I’ll open my mouth tomorrow.’” Ruth’s voice didn’t waver. “The young man hit him. Once. Here.” She touched her temple. “Vincent fell. He hit the corner of the table. He didn’t get up.”

“And you?”

“I screamed. The young man looked at me—really looked, like he was deciding something—and then he said, ‘Tell them he fell. Tell them he was drunk.’ And they left.”

“You didn’t call 911?”

“I did. After twenty minutes. I told them he’d fallen. I told the officers the same thing. They believed me. Why wouldn’t they? An old woman, a dead husband, a bottle of whiskey on the table that I put there myself.”

Reyes was quiet.

“Why now?” he finally asked.

Ruth set down the cup. “Because I saw the young man yesterday. On the news. He’s a councilman now. Smiling. Shaking hands. And I thought—Vincent opened the wrong door, but I closed the right one. And I’ve been sitting behind it ever since.”

She stood, straightened her rain bonnet. “You can write it down or not. But I’ve said it now. And it’s true.”

Reyes watched her walk out into the rain. Then he picked up his pen and wrote the date at the top of a fresh page.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The Bell & Anchor hadn’t changed. Same sticky floor. Same smell of stale beer and fried onions. Same dim lighting that hid the cracks in the vinyl booths.

I was two sips into a whiskey I didn’t need when the door opened and let in the cold.

He walked in like he owned the place. Maybe he did now. Danny McCabe. The boy I’d left behind without a note, without a call, without a goddamn word.

He looked older. We all did. But it was more than that. The softness was gone from his jaw. His shoulders filled out his jacket in a way that said he’d spent the last ten years doing something more than pushing paper. He scanned the room. His eyes found mine and stopped.

I didn’t look away. That would’ve been an admission. I just lifted my glass and took another sip, let the burn settle in my chest.

He walked over. Slow. Deliberate. Like he had all the time in the world and I was the one who’d have to wait.

“Well,” he said. “Look what the cat dragged in.”

His voice was the same. Low. Rough around the edges. It hit me somewhere below the ribs.

“Danny.”

“That’s all you got? My name?” He slid into the booth across from me without asking. “Ten years and that’s the opener?”

“What do you want me to say? Sorry for leaving? Sorry I didn’t write?” I set my glass down harder than I meant to. “I was eighteen. I was scared. I was a lot of things.”

“You were a coward.”

The word landed like a slap. I felt my jaw tighten.

“Yeah,” I said. “I was.”

He leaned back. Studied me. His eyes were still that impossible blue, the kind that made you feel like he could see right through your bullshit. Maybe he could.

“You’re back,” he said. Not a question.

“My mother’s sick.”

Something flickered in his face. Just for a second. Then it was gone.

“I heard. I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. She’s tough.” I took another drink. “She’ll outlive us all.”

“And you? You tough?”

“Tough enough.”

He nodded slowly. Like he was filing that away. “You writing for that paper in the city. I seen your byline.”

“You read my stuff?”

“Sometimes. When I can’t sleep.” He smirked. “You got a mean streak. I like it.”

“I learned from the best.”

That got a laugh out of him. Short. Sharp. It didn’t reach his eyes.

“So what now?” he asked. “You gonna run again when things get hard? Or you gonna stick around this time?”

I wanted to be angry. I wanted to tell him he didn’t know me anymore. But the truth was, he did. He knew the worst part of me. The part that ran. The part that was still running.

“I don’t know,” I said. And it was the most honest thing I’d said in years.

He reached across the table. His fingers brushed mine. Just barely. Just enough to make my breath catch.

“Well,” he said. “I guess we’ll find out.”

He stood up. Pulled a twenty from his wallet and dropped it on the table.

“Next round’s on me,” he said. “If you’re still here.”

Then he walked out. The door swung shut behind him. The cold crept back in.

I sat there for a long time. The whiskey was gone. The bar was empty. And I still didn’t know if I was going to stay or run.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The secure phone on Lena’s desk didn’t ring so much as it buzzed—a low, angry vibration that seemed to travel up her arm and settle in her teeth. She’d been staring at the same paragraph for ten minutes, the words on her screen blurring into a gray mush of acronyms and threat assessments. The caller ID was a string of digits she knew by heart: the Situation Room.

She snatched up the receiver. “Kessler.”

“Analyst Kessler, this is Deputy National Security Advisor Marsh. The President has a question about the PNK briefing you drafted.”

Lena’s spine straightened. The President. She’d spent three days on that brief, living on vending machine coffee and the grim satisfaction of connecting disparate dots into a coherent, terrifying picture. The PNK—Pyongyang’s new cyber-node—was a ghost, a phantom server farm that was siphoning intelligence from South Korean satellites. She’d found it. She’d named it.

“Of course, sir,” she said, her voice steadier than she felt. “What’s the question?”

“He’s concerned about the sourcing on the satellite intrusion vector. The chatter from the SIGINT intercepts. He wants to know if we have independent corroboration.”

A cold knot tightened in her stomach. “Sir, the intercepts were the corroboration. The primary source was the NIS asset in Busan. I was explicit about that in the brief. It’s the linchpin.”

There was a pause on the line, the kind that felt heavy with things unsaid. “Kessler, the brief we have in front of us says the primary sourcing was a low-confidence field report from a defector debriefed in Seoul six months ago. It mentions the NIS asset only as a peripheral data point.”

The world tilted. Lena gripped the edge of her desk, her knuckles turning white. “That’s not… that’s not what I wrote.” Her own voice sounded distant, hollow. “Sir, with respect, that’s a fundamental mischaracterization of the intelligence. The defector’s report was discredited. It’s why I flagged the NIS asset as the primary. The vector is real. The threat is imminent.”

“The President is about to authorize a retaliatory cyber-strike based on this brief, Kessler. He’s asking if we’re sure. And right now, the document in his hands suggests we are not. It suggests we’re acting on shaky ground.”

Her mind raced, a frantic scramble through the digital corridors of the last 72 hours. She’d sent the final draft to Marsh’s office for review, as per protocol. It had been approved. She had the email. But the version Marsh was reading… it was a masterpiece of subtle sabotage. It didn’t change the facts, it just… re-weighted them. It made the solid ground look like quicksand. It made her careful, nuanced analysis look like a reckless leap.

“Sir, I need you to pull the original file,” she said, her voice dropping to a low, urgent tone. “The one I sent to your office at 0400 this morning. Compare the metadata. Someone has altered the document.”

“That’s a serious accusation, Kessler.”

“It’s not an accusation, it’s a fact,” she shot back, the fear now transmuted into a cold, hard fury. “Someone is trying to derail this. They’re trying to make the President hesitate. They’re trying to make *me* look like I don’t know my job.” She took a breath, the pieces clicking into place with horrifying clarity. “Sir, who else had access to the draft between my send and the President’s morning briefing?”

The silence on the other end of the line was now charged with a new, darker electricity. She could almost hear the calculations happening in Marsh’s head. The political implications. The internal security nightmare.

“I’ll look into it,” Marsh said, his voice clipped. “For now, stay by your phone. Do not discuss this with anyone.”

The line went dead. Lena slowly hung up the receiver, the plastic slick with her sweat. She stared at her computer screen, at the paragraph she’d been reading. It was her analysis. But it wasn’t her voice. It was a lie, expertly crafted to look like the truth. The phantom server farm was real, but the ghost in the machine, she now realized, was inside the CIA. And it was standing right behind her.

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
The first shell hit the perimeter fence at 0430, a dull crump that rolled across the basin like distant thunder. Sergeant Kade Voss was already awake, sitting on the edge of his bunk with a mug of cold coffee, listening to the wind scrape the corrugated walls of the barracks. He set the mug down and pulled on his boots without hurry. Twenty-two years in armored cavalry had taught him that panic was a luxury for people who hadn't seen the morning's duty roster.

"Contact," the comm crackled. "Sector Four. Mortars, walking pattern. Looks like they're ranging."

Voss keyed his throat mic. "All crews, mount up. We're on the clock."

The mining colony of Tarsis-9 was a scab of rust and floodlights on a dead moon, three hundred souls and a processing plant that refined cesium for half the outer belt. The corporate charter had paid for a single understrength platoon of mercenary armor: four tanks, two of them older than their drivers, and a maintenance crew that drank more than it wrenched. The invaders—a syndicate outfit out of the Kessler Reach, according to intel that was probably three days stale—had brought a battalion.

Voss climbed into the turret of the *Iron Widow*, a battered Meridian-class MBT with a scar across its glacis from a previous contract and a main gun that had been rebuilt twice. His driver, a laconic woman named Hale, was already running the pre-start sequence. The engine coughed, caught, and settled into a deep, rattling idle that Voss felt in his teeth.

"Gunner," he said.

"Up," came the reply from below. Private First Class Okonkwo, nineteen years old and on his second contract, his voice steady in a way that Voss recognized as fear held in a tight fist.

"Load sabot. We're going hull-down on the ridge east of the plant. Hale, take us out slow. I want to hear the ground."

The *Iron Widow* lurched forward, tracks chewing through the loose regolith. Outside, the sky was a bruised purple, the colony's floodlights cutting hard white cones through the dust. The other three tanks fell into column behind them—*Grim Harvest*, *Bone Dry*, and *Little Murder*, the last a light recon vehicle that Okonkwo had once described as "a shopping cart with a gun."

The mortars had stopped. That was worse. Voss scanned the ridgeline through his optics, the thermal overlay painting the desert in shades of cold blue. Nothing moved. Then a flicker at the edge of the screen, a heat bloom that resolved into a shape.

"Contact, eleven o'clock, three kilometers. Tracked vehicle. Make that six tracked vehicles."

"Copy," Hale said. "They're spreading out. Classic envelopment."

"Let them come. Okonkwo, hold fire until I say. I want the lead vehicle in the kill zone before we open up."

The syndicate tanks were pushing forward in a loose wedge, their engines throwing up plumes of dust that caught the floodlights. Voss counted eight now, then ten. Behind them, the boxy silhouettes of armored personnel carriers, infantry clinging to the hulls. It was a lot of metal for a mining colony. Someone in the Kessler Reach had decided Tarsis-9 was worth taking, and they'd brought enough to do it.

"*Widow*, this is *Harvest*," the comm crackled. Sergeant Deke, older than Voss, twice as ugly, and the only man Voss trusted to hold a flank. "You seeing what I'm seeing?"

"Ten tanks, maybe a dozen carriers. They're not here to negotiate."

"Figured. You want me to take the left, you take the right?"

"No. I want you to fall back to the secondary line and cover the plant's north approach. If they break through there, we're done."

A pause. "You're splitting us."

"I'm covering the only thing that matters. The rest is just ground."

Deke grunted. "*Harvest* moving. Don't get yourself killed, Voss. I owe you money."

The first syndicate tank crossed the three-kilometer mark. Voss felt the *Widow* settle into the dirt, the stabilizers humming. Okonkwo's breathing was loud in the intercom, slow and deliberate, the way you breathed when you were trying not to think about the fact that the next few minutes would decide whether you lived.

"Steady," Voss said. "Wait for it."

Two kilometers. The lead tank's turret swung, searching. It hadn't found them yet. The ridge was low, barely a rise, but the *Widow* was hull-down, only the gun and the commander's cupola exposed. The syndicate crews were good—they were scanning, not just driving—but they were also arrogant. They'd expected a token defense, maybe a few autocannons and a lot of surrender.

"Okonkwo. Lead tank. Sabot. Fire."

The *Widow* slammed back on its suspension. The shell crossed the distance in a heartbeat, a flat crack that echoed off the basin walls, and the lead syndicate tank vanished in a blossom of orange and black. The turret lifted, spun, and came down twenty meters away.

"Hit," Okonkwo said, his voice thin. "Target destroyed."

"Second tank. Fire."

Another round. Another kill. The syndicate formation dissolved into chaos, vehicles slewing left and right, commanders screaming over open frequencies that Voss could hear bleeding through the comm. Then they found their spine. The remaining tanks opened up, shells walking toward the ridge, throwing up geysers of dirt and rock.

"*Bone Dry*, shifting left," came the call. "They're trying to flank us."

"Let them," Voss said. "Okonkwo, keep firing. Hale, back us up fifty meters and shift right. I want them to think we're falling back."

The *Widow* reversed, tracks grinding, and the syndicate tanks pressed forward, hungry now, confident. That was the mistake. When they crested the ridge, *Bone Dry* and *Little Murder* were waiting in the shadows of the processing plant, guns already laid.

The fight lasted another eleven minutes. When it was over, seven syndicate tanks were burning, three had retreated, and the desert was littered with the wreckage of armored personnel carriers. The *Widow* had taken two hits, neither penetrating, and Okonkwo was shaking so badly he could barely reload.

Voss climbed out of the turret and stood on the hull, looking at the smoke. Hale joined him, wiping grease from her hands.

"They'll come back," she said.

"Probably." Voss pulled a crumpled cigarette from his pocket and lit it. "But not today. Today they learned what it costs."

Behind them, the floodlights of Tarsis-9 burned on, steady and indifferent, and the processing plant hummed its endless song.

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The blizzard had been a rumor on the radio at noon and a hard fact by four. Dr. Ellie Vance was stitching a laceration on a quarter horse named Bandit when the power went out, and she finished the last three knots by the light of her phone flashlight, which she held in her teeth. Bandit, to his credit, stood like a gentleman.

“You’re a better patient than most men I know,” she told the horse, snapping off her gloves.

She had no business being out here. The Lazy K was forty minutes from town on a good day, and this was not a good day. But Cal Kincaid had called at three, his voice flat and unbothered the way it always was, and said he had a horse that needed seeing to, and Ellie had said she’d come. She always said she’d come. That was the trouble with her, or one of the troubles.

By the time she had Bandit settled and her kit packed, the windows were white. Not frosted—white, like someone had painted over them from the outside. The wind made a sound she didn’t like, a low howl that got into the walls.

Cal appeared in the barn doorway, snow in his eyebrows. He was sixty-one years old and built like a fence post, all length and stubbornness, and he looked at her the way he looked at weather he couldn’t do anything about.

“You’re not driving home,” he said.

“I’ve got chains.”

“You’ve got a rear-wheel-drive pickup and a death wish. Road’s gone. Come up to the house.”

She wanted to argue. She was good at arguing; it was practically a hobby. But the wind chose that moment to slam the barn door against its frame, and Bandit skittered in his stall, and Ellie thought about the drop-off past the cattle guard, the one with no guardrail and no forgiveness.

“Fine,” she said.

The house was warm and cluttered and smelled like woodsmoke and coffee left too long on the burner. Cal fed the stove, and she stood in the kitchen with her coat still on, dripping on his floor, and he didn’t tell her to take it off, just handed her a towel and a mug.

“It’s instant,” he said.

“I noticed.”

They drank their coffee standing up, listening to the storm. It was, Ellie thought, the longest they’d been in a room together without a horse between them. Six years she’d been coming out to this ranch. Six years of him calling her ma’am and her calling him Mr. Kincaid, and once, two winters back, a bad night with a colicking mare when they’d sat on hay bales until dawn and he’d told her about his wife, Ruth, dead eleven years now, and how she’d planted the lilacs by the porch that never bloomed worth a damn.

“The lilacs,” she said now, for no reason.

Cal looked at her. “What about them.”

“They ever bloom?”

“No.” He set his mug down. “Ruth planted them wrong. Too much shade. I never told her. Figured she’d want to believe they might.”

Ellie laughed, and it surprised them both. Cal’s mouth did something complicated, a smile that had rusted from lack of use.

The power stayed out. He found candles, the real kind, and she sat in his living room in borrowed wool socks while he built up the fire. The wind rattled the windows and the snow climbed the porch steps and somewhere in the barn Bandit was warm and fed and fine, and Ellie felt the strange, unhurried quiet of being exactly where she couldn’t leave.

“You could sell the place,” she said. “Move to town.”

“Could.”

“But you won’t.”

“No.” He poked the fire. “Ruth’s in the walls. Can’t get her out.”

It wasn’t a sad thing the way he said it. Just true, like the weather.

She woke on the couch under a quilt that smelled like cedar, and the storm had passed. The world outside was white and still and enormous. Cal was already in the kitchen, and there was bacon, and he’d found the good coffee somewhere, and he looked at her across the counter and said, “Roads’ll be cleared by noon.”

“I know,” she said.

Neither of them mentioned the lilacs again. But in the spring, she thought, she might drive out and take a look at that shade.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The red ON AIR light cast a bloody glow across the cramped studio. Vince “The Fang” Moreau leaned back in his worn leather chair, headphones clamped over his ears, and watched the caller line blink.

“You’re on Night Howl with Vince Moreau,” he growled, his voice a low rumble that had made housewives in three counties clutch their pearls. “What’s got you up at this ungodly hour, sweetheart?”

A pause. Then a man’s voice, flat and cold. “I’m a hunter.”

Vince’s claw-tipped fingers stilled on the mixing board. He’d been doing this show for six years—three of them as a werewolf—and he’d heard every kind of crazy. But something about the delivery made his hackles rise.

“A hunter,” Vince repeated, letting the word hang. “Like deer? Duck? Big game?”

“You know what I hunt.”

The studio’s AC hummed. Vince glanced at the soundproof window, where his producer, a nervous rabbit shifter named Delia, was already scribbling on a notepad. She held it up: *CUT HIM OFF?*

Vince shook his head. “Alright, pal. You got a name, or do I just call you ‘The Hunter’? Sounds like a bad action movie.”

“Call me what you want. I’ve been tracking your kind for fifteen years.”

“My kind.” Vince felt his canines lengthen a fraction. He forced them back. “You mean radio hosts? We’re a vicious breed, I’ll give you that. Once talked a guy’s ear off about the mating habits of moths for forty-five minutes.”

The hunter didn’t laugh. “You think this is funny? I’ve got silver bullets in my glove box and a map with three pack dens circled in red. You want to know how many werewolves I’ve put down?”

Vince’s good humor evaporated. He sat forward, elbows on the desk. “You know what I think? I think you’re a lonely guy with a six-pack and a grudge. But since you called my show, you get my time. So go ahead—what’s your beef with the furries?”

“They killed my brother.”

The words landed like a slap. Vince exhaled slowly. “When?”

“Three years ago. Full moon. He was camping in the Black Hills. They didn’t even leave enough to bury.”

Vince closed his eyes. He knew the Black Hills pack. Rough crowd, but they had rules. Accidents happened, sure—new turns, bad moons, territorial disputes. But a full-on slaughter? That was execution. And if this hunter was telling the truth, someone had broken the code.

“I’m sorry about your brother,” Vince said, and meant it. “But you’re talking to a guy who does a call-in show about supernatural gossip and plays classic rock. I’m not the alpha of anything. I don’t run with a pack.”

“You’re a werewolf.”

“And you’re a hunter. We’ve established the obvious. What’s your endgame here? You gonna come down to the station and shoot me live on air? Ratings would be killer, but Delia’s got a thing about blood on the carpet.”

The hunter’s voice dropped. “I’m not coming for you. Not yet. I called because I wanted to hear it. The voice of the monster. I wanted to know if you sounded like a man.”

“And?”

“You sound like a late-night DJ who thinks he’s funny.”

Vince snorted. “That’s fair. But here’s the thing, pal—you think hunting us makes you righteous. But I’ve met hunters who were worse than any wolf. I’ve seen a guy skin a shifter alive for the bounty. You want to talk about monsters? Let’s talk about the ones who hunt for sport.”

Silence. Then, quietly: “You don’t know me.”

“No. I don’t. But I know grief. It rots you from the inside. You keep buying silver and drawing maps, you’re gonna wake up one day and realize you’ve become the thing you hate. I’ve seen it happen. Wolf or human—doesn’t matter. The chase eats you.”

The hunter laughed, a dry, humorless sound. “You’re giving me therapy now? That’s rich.”

“I’m giving you the truth. You called a werewolf radio host at two in the morning. You wanted somebody to talk to. So talk. What was your brother’s name?”

A long pause. Vince heard the crackle of a cigarette being lit.

“…Tommy.”

“Tommy. Okay. What’d he do? Before?”

“He was a mechanic. Loved fishing. Had a lousy singing voice.”

Vince smiled despite himself. “Sounds like my kind of guy. You know what I do on Sundays? I go to the diner on Fifth and order the meatloaf. The waitress there, Marge—she’s a banshee. Knows everyone’s death day. She told me I’d go out choking on a chicken bone at eighty-nine. That’s the kind of monster I am. Terrifying, right?”

The hunter didn’t respond. Vince could hear him breathing, the faint crackle of the cigarette.

“Look,” Vince said. “I’m not gonna convince you to drop your silver. But if you ever want to talk again—without the threats—call the station. I’m here every Thursday, midnight to three. Bring a song request. I take dedications.”

“You’re insane.”

“Probably. But I’m also the only werewolf you’ve ever met who’ll play Bon Jovi for you. Think about it.”

A click. The line went dead.

Vince pulled off his headphones and rubbed his face. Delia appeared in the doorway, eyes wide.

“That was terrifying,” she whispered.

“Yeah.” Vince reached for the next caller button. “But he’ll call back. They always do.”

He flicked the switch. “You’re on Night Howl. What’s your request?”

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
The diary was bound in cheap red vinyl, the kind you’d find at a drugstore. It was tucked in the back of his sock drawer, under a pile of tube socks he never wore. My hands trembled as I opened it.

The first entry was dated eight months ago.

*I found the gun today.*

I stopped breathing. The words blurred. I blinked hard and forced myself to keep reading.

*It was in the garage, way back on the top shelf behind the paint cans. A little revolver. He thinks I don’t know. He thinks I’m stupid. Maybe I am. Maybe I’m stupid for staying. But I’m not blind.*

I flipped ahead. The handwriting got messier, more frantic. The neat loops turned into sharp, jagged slashes.

*He was out late again. Said it was work. I called the office. The night janitor answered. Said nobody’s been there since five. So where were you, Michael? Where were you?*

My jaw tightened. I remembered that night. I’d told her I was working late. I’d actually been at my brother’s place, drinking too much and complaining about my marriage. I never told her that.

The next page was worse.

*I followed him. I’m not proud of it. But I did. He went to a bar on 5th. He sat in the corner. He didn’t talk to anyone. He just drank. Two whiskeys. Neat. And then he cried. Right there at the bar. My husband cried and I watched him from my car like some kind of creep. I wanted to go in. I wanted to hold him. But I didn’t. I drove home and pretended I didn’t see.*

My throat felt tight. I didn’t remember crying at that bar. I remembered the whiskey. I remembered the numbness. The rest was a blur.

The entries got shorter. Darker. She wrote about the pills she found in his jacket pocket. The way he’d stopped eating dinner with her. The way he’d flinch when she touched him.

*He’s slipping away from me. I can feel it. It’s like watching someone drown in slow motion. I’m standing right there on the shore and I can’t reach him. I don’t know how to swim.*

Then, two months ago, a single line.

*I think he’s having an affair.*

My stomach dropped. I wanted to throw the book across the room. I wanted to burn it. But I couldn’t stop reading.

*There’s a woman at his office. Sarah. She calls him. He smiles when he talks to her. Not the fake smile he gives me. The real one. The one that used to be mine.*

I didn’t even know a Sarah. I never had an affair. I never even thought about it. The only woman at my office was a sixty-year-old receptionist named Brenda. She brought in homemade cookies on Fridays.

The final entry was dated three days before the accident. The handwriting was almost unreadable. The pen had dug into the paper.

*I can’t do this anymore. I can’t watch him destroy himself. I can’t be the one who finds him. I won’t be. I told him I’d leave. I told him I was done. I didn’t mean it. I just wanted him to fight. To say something. To prove he still loved me. He just looked at me. He didn’t say a word. He just looked at me with those empty eyes and then he went to the garage.*

I closed the book. My hands were shaking. I stared at the red vinyl cover. She thought I was having an affair. She thought I didn’t love her. She thought I was already gone.

And the whole time, I was just trying to figure out how to tell her I’d lost my job six months ago.

title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
The officer’s name was Patterson, and he was young enough to be her grandson. He sat on the edge of her floral-print sofa, his back straight, his notebook open on his knee, and he had the kind of face that hadn’t yet learned how to hide its skepticism. He’d been polite, even gentle, when he’d arrived, but she could see the official version of the story settling behind his eyes like silt.

“Mrs. Gable,” he said, his pen poised. “The report from that night says you told the responding officers you were asleep. That you didn’t hear anything until the ambulance arrived.”

Eleanor Gable looked past him, out the window to where her hydrangeas were blooming in a riot of impossible blue. They had been Arthur’s, once. He’d fed them coffee grounds and eggshells, and he’d talked to them, a low, rumbling monologue that had always made her smile.

“I lied,” she said. The word felt foreign in her mouth, a small, hard stone she’d carried for forty years. Patterson’s pen stopped moving. He looked up, his gaze sharpening. “I wasn’t asleep. I was in the kitchen.”

“The kitchen,” he repeated, writing it down. “And your husband, Arthur, he was…?”

“He was in the garage. With the car.” She paused, the memory rising not as a picture, but as a collection of sensations: the smell of gasoline and old wood, the chill of the concrete floor through her slippers, the heavy, suffocating silence. “He’d been drinking. Not a lot, not that night. But enough. He’d been out there for an hour, tinkering. He said the engine was making a funny noise.”

She had gone out to check on him. The garage door was up, and the overhead light was on, casting a sickly yellow glow on the workbench, the coiled garden hose, the neat rows of tools. Arthur was sitting in the driver’s seat, the engine idling, a smooth, contented purr. The garage door was closed. The overhead light was off. The only light came from the car’s dashboard, a faint, greenish luminescence that lit the planes of his face.

“He was just sitting there,” Eleanor said, her voice quiet but steady. “Listening to the radio. He had it on low, some jazz program. He looked… peaceful. He looked like he was already gone.”

Patterson’s pen scratched across the page. “And you didn’t think to open the door? To turn off the engine?”

“I did open the door. I stood there for a long time, watching him. He didn’t see me.” She remembered the weight of the door handle in her hand, the squeak of the hinge. She remembered the smell, thick and sweet and final. “I stood there and I thought about all the years. The good ones, and the bad ones. The way he’d laugh, and the way he’d go quiet for days. I thought about how tired I was. How tired we both were.”

The officer was silent, his pen resting on the page. The only sound was the ticking of the grandfather clock in the hall, a wedding gift from a long-dead aunt.

“I closed the door,” Eleanor said, meeting his eyes for the first time. “I pulled it shut, and I went back into the house. I made myself a cup of tea. I sat at the kitchen table and I drank it. It was Earl Grey. It was hot. I could hear the muffled sound of the engine through the wall. And then, after a while, I couldn’t hear it anymore.”

She paused, letting the silence hang in the air between them. Patterson didn’t look skeptical anymore. He looked, she thought, a little bit lost.

“I finished my tea,” she continued, her voice barely a whisper. “I washed the cup. I dried it. I put it away. And then I went to the phone and I called for help.” She looked down at her own hands, spotted and veined, resting in her lap. “I told them I’d just woken up. That I didn’t know what was wrong. I told them the truth, you see. Just not all of it.”
